[[RunningHead]]

A Discussion of “De-Pathologizing Homosexuality”; A Presentation by Lawrence Hartmann, MD, to the New York Psychoanalytic Society November 2024

Mark Smaller PHD

Mark Smaller

P.O. Box 9, Douglas, MI 49406
marksmaller@gmail.com

Mark Smaller   Adult, adolescent and child psychoanalyst, is a past president of the American Psychoanalytic Association and a former two-term board member of the International Psychoanalytic Association.
Homosexuality, psychoanalytic institutions, organizational change, diagnosis and power, apology and repair

This discussion offers a response to Dr Lawrence Hartmann’s lecture on the history of de-pathologizing homosexuality within psychoanalysis. While commending Dr Hartmann’s thorough and courageous account, I reflect on the profession’s painful slowness to enact change. Drawing from my own experience – as a past president of the American Psychoanalytic Association (APsaA), a former board member of the International Psychoanalytic Association (IPA), and a clinician – I trace the resistance and eventual evolution within psychoanalytic institutions, particularly APsaA, from discrimination to formal apology. I share personal encounters, including the pivotal moment of Dr Richard Isay’s talk in 1991, and reflect on the systemic and subjective factors that sustained harmful diagnostic practices. I examine how the institutional resistance to change – when fueled by misuse of theory and unconscious dynamics – threatens not only the integrity of our field but its future relevance. Finally, I argue that organizational apologies, while insufficient alone, are necessary starting points for transformation. Dr Hartmann’s talk reminds us of what psychoanalysis can become when it acts in alignment with its deepest values.

[[RunningHead]]

Development as a Multi-Systemic Endeavor: Personal and Professional Reflections on S. J. Blatt’s Philosophy of Development

Golan Shahar PHD and Linda C. Mayes MD

Linda C. Mayes

800 Ben-Gurion Avenue, Beer-Sheva 84105, Israel
Golan.shahar878@gmail.com

Linda C. Mayes   Developmental pediatrician and child and adult psychoanalyst. She is the Arnold Gesell Professor of Child Psychiatry, Pediatrics, and Psychology and Chair of the Yale Child Study Center, Yale School of Medicine.
Sidney Blatt, development, psychoanalysis, philosophy, object-relations

We offer personal (life-story based) and professional (theoretical, empirical) reflections on Sidney J. Blatt’s philosophy of human development. By philosophy, we mean the very metaphysical assumptions about human nature and its development throughout the life span, which guided Blatt’s seminal contribution to the areas of psychoanalysis, developmental psychology and psychopathology. Of the various assumptions we discuss, we title the most central one is “multi-systemic development.” Namely, Blatt’s thinking was adamantly broad, as he strongly believed that to understand the developing mind, one has to put together all components of the person’s upbringing, personality, and life circumstances. Such holistic thinking enabled Blatt to make connections between seemingly unrelated areas of scholarship, and – in turn – to arrive at, arguably, the most comprehensive theory of psychological development in academic psychology.

Rachel B. Blass PHD

Rachel B. Blass

13 Gikhon Street, Jerusalem 93454713, Israel
rachelblass@gmail.com

Rachel B. Blass   Member and Training Analyst at the Israel Psychoanalytic Society and a member of the British Psychoanalytical Society.
Economic model, Draft G, longing, Freud, metapsychology, Mourning and Melancholia

In this paper, I show how the failure of Freud’s efforts to understand the phenomenon of depression in economic terms played an important role in the development of his object relational understanding of the person. That is, that the experience of depression, not well encompassed by energetic terms and the pleasure principle with which it is so strongly associated, compelled Freud to ground his thinking in a metapsychological model that is more relational, one in which maintaining relationships, rather than the attainment of personal pleasure through the lowering of excitation, is a central motivating force.

[[RunningHead]]

The Contributions of Sidney J. Blatt to Understanding Conscious and Unconscious Aspects of Mental Representation: Narrative Descriptions and Dream Narratives

Diana Diamond PHD and John S. Auerbach PHD

John S. Auerbach

135 Central Park West, Suite 1N, New York, NY 10023
ddiamonda@gmail.com

John S. Auerbach   Professor of Psychology at Nova Southeastern University.
Mental representation, object relations, manifest dream, latent content, self-other differentiation relatedness

This paper, written in honor of Sidney Blatt, explores how object relations are represented in narrative descriptions and in dream narratives and discusses how changes in these two assessments of object relations diverge or converge over the course of treatment. As part of Blatt’s Object Representation Research Group (ORRG) at the Yale University School of Medicine, Diamond and colleagues developed the Differentiation-Relatedness (D-R) Scale to assess the developmental level of mental representations as evidenced in spontaneous descriptions of self and significant others on the Object Relations Inventory (ORI). The D-R Scale focuses on self-definition and relatedness, the two developmental lines that in Blatt’s view drive the development and internalization of mental representations, in self and other. This study presents both clinical and extraclinical data on one patient, part of a larger sample of 40 who were systematically assessed for changes in D-R over the course of long-term psychoanalytically oriented inpatient treatment. In addition, this patient’s dream narratives were assessed for object relations with the Object Representation Scale for Dreams (ORSD). The results indicated that this patient moved from unilateral polarized or split descriptions of self and others on the ORI to more complex, balanced modulated and multifaceted descriptions at discharge (2 years, 9 months). Parallel improvements in the developmental level and quality of object relations were observed in the dream narrations. These changes suggest that transformations of the capacity to represent objects at both conscious and unconscious levels may be proxies for change in psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy.

Changes in Self and Object Representations as Measured by the Differentiation-Relatedness Scale in Patients with a Personality Disorder During a Hospitalization-Based Psychodynamic Treatment

Benedicte Lowyck PHD , Yannic Verhaest MA , Rudi Vermote MD PHD and Patrick Luyten PHD

Patrick Luyten

Campus Kortenberg, Leuvensesteenweg 517, Kortenberg 3070, Belgium
benedicte.lowyck@kuleuven.be

Patrick Luyten   Professor at the Faculty of Psychology and Educational Sciences, University of Leuven, Belgium, and at the Research Department of Clinical, Educational and Health Psychology, University College London, United Kingdom.
Differentiation-Relatedness Scale (DRS), personality disorder, Object Relations Inventory (ORI), self and object representations

The Differentiation-Relatedness Scale (DRS) as scored on the Object Relations Inventory (ORI) assesses the level of differentiation and relatedness in mental representations of self and significant others. The current study focuses on changes in mental representations of self and significant others (mother, father, and therapist) in patients with a personality disorder (PD) during a hospitalization-based psychodynamic treatment. Here, we summarize the results of two studies. The first study was part of the Kortenberg-Leuven process-outcome study I, and included 35 PD patients who completed the ORI and other measures at intake, 3, 6, and 9 months into treatment, at discharge, and at 3-month and 1-year follow-up. The second study reports preliminary results of the Kortenberg-Leuven process-outcome II study in a sample 68 PD patients, investigating change in the levels of differentiation and relatedness of object representations from intake to treatment termination. Results of both studies showed significant improvements in levels of differentiation and relatedness between intake and discharge. In particular, PD patients moved from mental representations characterized by polarization and the use of splitting on the DRS (DRS level = 5) to emergent object constancy and ambivalence tolerance, and thus to more stable and coherent mental representations of both self and significant others (DRS level = 6). In addition, improvements in mental representations of self as well as mother, father, and therapist were maintained at follow-up.

Differences in Self and Other Representations in Inpatients Diagnosed with Depression, Borderline Personality Disorder, and Psychotic Disorders: A Test of Blatt’s Model

Kenneth N. Levy PHD , Kevin B. Meehan PHD and Paul H. Tullis PHD

Paul H. Tullis

362 Bruce V. Moore Building, 138 Fischer Road, University Park, PA 16802
klevy@psu.edu

Paul H. Tullis   Psychologist at the William C. Tallent VA Outpatient Clinic for the U.S. Department of Veteran Affairs.
Personality organization, mental representations, borderline personality disorder, psychosis, depression

Psychoanalytic theorists contend that severe psychopathology involves fundamental disturbances in self- and object representations. Kernberg distinguishes between neurotic, borderline, and psychotic levels of personality organization based on the degree of differentiation and integration of self and object representations. Blatt developed the Object Relations Inventory (ORI) for assessing the structure of mental representations by evaluating open-ended descriptions of self and significant others. In the present study we examine the relationship of mental representations to clinical diagnosis (i.e. neurotic, borderline, and psychotic). Participants were 76 (41 men, 35 women) young adult and adolescent psychiatric inpatients, ages ranging from 13 to 26 (median = 16). Participants were reliably diagnosed with psychotic disorders (n = 12), borderline personality disorder (n = 43), or depression (n = 21) and assessed with the ORI. Consistent with our main hypotheses, results suggest a progression in the developmental level of mental representations, though primarily between patients with psychotic versus neurotic and borderline diagnoses. While limited by the small sample size, the implications of findings for psychodynamic models of psychopathology are discussed.

Eating disorders, anorexia nervosa, sense of self, psychotherapy for eating disorders, object representation, inner world

This paper illustrates the interplay of research and psychological treatment in the author’s work with eating-disorder patients. The mutual influence of research and clinical treatment was valued and encouraged by Sidney Blatt. A literature review includes both clinical and research reports of the inner world of eating-disorder patients. An outline follows of the author’s previously published research on the sense of self and object representations of hospitalized anorexia-nervosa patients aged 14 to 24, and a new qualitative analysis of some of that data. The author then describes the psychotherapy of a young adult, female, eating-disorder patient, during which treatment the research results promoted the exploration of the patient’s inner world of self and object representations, while her symptoms abated, and aspects of her life changed.

Therapeutic Alliance and Ruptures in Three Psychoanalytic Dyads: An Exploratory Investigation

Nadine J. Kaslow PHD ABPP , Stefanie Speanburg PHD LCSW , Shweta Kapoor MD PHD , William Howard Hudson MD , Heather Key Domingue PHD , Sheril Kalarithara MD , Courtney L. Crooks PHD and Andrea L. Crowell MD

Andrea L. Crowell

80 Jesse Hill Jr. Drive, Atlanta, GA 30303
nkaslow@emory.edu
http://orcid.org/0000-0003-0775-8597

Andrea L. Crowell   Assistant Professor at the Emory University School of Medicine, Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences.
Therapeutic alliance, therapeutic ruptures, transference-countertransference, creative writers, qualitative methods

The therapeutic alliance is frequently cited as one of the most critically important common factors associated with therapeutic outcomes. While ruptures to the therapeutic alliance are inevitable in all treatments, more research is needed to investigate the contributions of both the psychotherapist and the patient in effectively repairing these ruptures in a manner that facilitates therapeutic progress. In appreciation of Sidney Blatt’s research demonstrating the powerful role that the therapeutic alliance plays in determining therapeutic outcomes, this exploratory report examines transcripts from the beginning, middle, and end phases of the analyses of three creative writers with a focus on the therapeutic alliance and therapeutic ruptures as related to transference-countertransference dynamics. The Collaborative Interactions Scale – Revised (CIS-R) was the coding system used to rate the analysands’ Direct Rupture Markers, Indirect Rupture Markers, Direct Collaborative Processes, and Indirect Collaborative Processes and the analysts’ Direct Collaborative Interventions, Indirect Collaborative Interventions, Rupture Interventions, and Form of Therapist Intervention. The key findings, which support the theoretical and empirical work of Blatt and colleagues, are as follows: (1) most of the analysand-analyst interactions were indirect, rather than direct, in nature; (2) the analyst’s used many supportive interventions in addition to more classic exploratory and expressive ones: (3) the presence of rupture markers was limited and the reflections of ruptures was primarily indirect and included affective withdrawal and verbal avoidance; and (4) analysands may make important and unique contributions to the rupture process. The empirical and clinical implications of the results are discussed.

Sidney J. Blatt, PhD: His Contributions to Formulating Progress in Psychoanalysis

Barbara F. Marcus PHD

Barbara F. Marcus

234 Church Street, Suite 300, New Haven, CT 06510-1802
Barbara.marcus@yale.edu

Barbara F. Marcus   Assistant Clinical Professor in the Department of Psychiatry at the Yale University School of Medicine and a Training and Supervising Analyst at The Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis.
Experienced incompatibility, gratifying involvement, internalization, interpretation, therapeutic action

Blatt’s novel model of therapeutic action is among his most significant contributions to psychoanalytic theory. Together with collaborator Rebecca Behrends, their reformulation offered a unique integration of both key historical traditions and psychoanalytic developmental theory and research. Inspired by the work of their mentor and colleague Hans Loewald, they viewed internalization as the over-arching principle of psychic development throughout the life cycle. Applying a Piagetian framework, they view internalized object relations as becoming progressively more differentiated, articulated, and integrated, facilitating increasingly more advanced ego development and mature relatedness. Unlike many of their predecessors, Blatt and Behrends regarded the parent’s resonance with the child as necessary, but not sufficient. Drawing on the work of George Klein, they posited that inevitable cycles of gratifying involvement, tolerable moments of experienced incompatibility, and the restitution of attunement are the fundamental catalyst for internalization and psychic advancement. Analogously, Blatt and Behrends proposed a model of therapeutic action that parallels these developmental cycles. Through accurate and empathic transference interpretation, the analysand internalizes the analyst’s reflective functioning and psychological growth is kindled. Challenging the dominant zeitgeist of the time, they argued that the mutative effect of analysis depends equally on the cycles of gratifying involvement and interpretation. An extended clinical vignette illustrates the power and utility of the Blatt-Behrends model to formulate the course of a challenging yet productive analytic process. The significance and continued vitality of their novel, integrative model is discussed. Further theoretical questions, both developmental and technical, are raised for future consideration.

Cleavages, Rifts, and Discontinuities: An Exploration of Blatt and Behrends’ Model of Internalization

Kay M. Long PHD

Kay M. Long

180 East Rock Road, New Haven, CT 06511
kay.long@yale.edu

Kay M. Long   Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine and a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis.
Internalization, therapeutic action, experienced incompatibilities, projection, projective identification, interpretation

This paper explores the nature of therapeutic action in a patient whose capacity for internalization was compromised. Drawing on and extending the work of Blatt and Behrends on the role of internalization in therapeutic action, the author presents the case of a patient whose defensive responses to the discontinuities in the therapeutic relationship, “experienced incompatibilities” in Blatt and Behrends’ model, complicated her ability to take in and make use of what the analyst offered. Elaborating on Blatt and Behrends’ understanding of the role of interpretation in therapeutic action, the author illustrates some technical approaches to working with patients who employ defenses aimed at thwarting internalization.

Internalizing the Legacy of Sidney J. Blatt: Discussion of Papers by Barbara Marcus, Kay Long, and Susan Bers

John S. Auerbach PHD

John S. Auerbach

3300 South University Drive, Fort Lauderdale, FL 33328
jauerba1@nova.edu

John S. Auerbach   Clinical-Community Psychology at the State University of New York at Buffalo and is currently a Full Professor in the Department of Clinical and School Psychology at Nova Southeastern University.
Internalization, 2-configurations model, Object Relations Inventory, Differentiation-Relatedness Scale, attachment

This paper discusses the respective contributions of Marcus, Long, and Bers with regard to internalization, a central concept in the work of Sidney J. Blatt. Although importance of internalization in Blatt’s work, especially in his papers with Rebecca Behrends, and in psychoanalysis more generally is acknowledged, various problematic aspects of this concept, rooted in the subject-object problem in philosophy, are discussed. A dyadic-systems perspective and recent findings on mirror neurons are recommended for reconceptualizing this matter. The role of internalization in clinical cases by Marcus and by Long is examined, and it is noted that, although both of them work with developmentally traumatized patients, their respective understandings of the concept diverge considerably. Marcus focuses on relational aspects of internalization that derive from separations and reunions in the analytic process. By contrast, Long emphasizes interpretation, especially of envious and destructive wishes, as central to the internalization process in treatment. Finally, Bers presents empirical data demonstrating the content of internalizations, specifically differentiation-relatedness in patients with anorexia nervosa. She uses descriptions of self and others collected with the Object Relations Inventory to demonstrate self-critical hyperreflectivity and a negative, enmeshed relationship with mother in a young woman carrying this diagnosis. The discussant recommends reconceptualization of anorexia nervosa in terms of attachment styles, in particular avoidant-dismissive attachment. The importance of long-term relationships in the life and thought of Sidney Blatt and his many colleagues and mentees is discussed.

[[RunningHead]]

To My Dad – May 15, 2014 – with Love

David Blatt J.D.

David Blatt

2836 Albemarle Street NW, Washington, DC 20008
dblatt@wc.com

David Blatt   An attorney in Washington, D.C., who has a B.A. and J.D. from Yale (1985, 1988).

Thank you everyone for coming. On behalf of my sisters Sue and Judi, our mom Ethel, our spouses Charlie John and Lisa, all 9 grandchildren, and my dad’s brother Merwin, we appreciate your honoring Sid by being here today.

Many of you knew my Dad in many different contexts – some as a relative, some as a friend, some as a teacher, mentor, or colleague. Virtually everyone here knows the list of his professional accomplishments: a professor at Yale for more than 50 years; author or coauthor of more than 220 papers and 17 books; my Dad wrote on psychology, art history, and current events; he held distinguished visiting professorships at universities around the world; he mentored scores of graduate and post-graduate students; and received too many awards to list. He was a giant in his field – what we’d call a 5-tool player – an incredibly talented researcher, writer, teacher, mentor, and therapist. Of the five, his students were his top priority. They were family to him, and his relationships with his students and former students were a source of enormous joy. He immensely valued the collaborations he continued to have with his students after they became professors themselves, and he so appreciated the celebrations that his former students put together for him over the years.

But, what I’d really like to talk about today is my Dad as a person and as a father.

When my sisters and I spoke earlier this week with the rabbi about our father, he told us that he had talked with my Dad over the past year about many things, including my mom and us kids. And then he said, unsolicited: “Your father was a complicated man.” That is a very apt description of my Dad. In some ways, he was a man of great contradictions. For all his accomplishments, he was deeply insecure. I recall him telling me decades ago about his professional insecurities, that he sometimes doubted he was good enough to be a Yale professor, not good enough to merit the recognition he was receiving, that someone one day would discover that he was really not that talented.

Reflections from Sidney’s Granddaughter

Ruth Schwab

Ruth Schwab

311 Vista De Valle, Mill Valley, CA 94941
ruthieschwab@alumni.gsb.stanford.edu

Ruth Schwab   One of Sidney Blatt’s nine grandchildren. She currently works in technical product management at Amazon’s Worldwide Grocery Stores organization. Prior to Amazon, she worked at Google, Walmart, and Vermont Community Foundation in various capacities to improve sustainability and accessibility within the food industry. Ruth has an MBA from Stanford Graduate School of Business, an MS from Stanford’s Emmett Interdisciplinary Program in Environment and Resources, and a BA from Princeton University in Ecology and Evolutionary Biology, with a certificate in Studio Art.

I agreed to share slightly modified remarks from my grandfather’s memorial for this issue to represent a more personal side to Sidney and to work through my own reflections since his death on what it means to be a Blatt.

It’s hard to believe Pop has been gone for over ten years now (a mischievous impulse led me to shorten our standard Grandpop moniker to “Pop,” once, and he’d unexpectedly embraced the endearment). So much of who I am I can attribute to him – either how he and Grandmom raised my mother Susan or how they shaped my childhood directly. I grew up in the same small town outside New Haven where they’d lived most of their years prior to Whitney Center, and they were very much a part of my life. While I didn’t have the same pressures as the Blatt children, it was always clear to me that, as part of the family, I was expected to achieve greatness. I could be a doctor, a lawyer, an artist, a hairdresser – but whatever it was I had to be the best one out there. From my grandfather, I learned three main things:

Aim beyond what I think I can achieve

Never take no for an answer

Follow my passion

These were concepts he lived by that I learned from example.

Pop expected me to aim high. I know I’m not alone in that; he challenged his relatives, students, and colleagues alike. I’m sure all the Blatt kids have stories of bringing home a test where they’d set the curve for the class or gotten a 99%, only for Sidney to inquire, “so, what did you get wrong?” It was clear to me from an early age that achievement in our family was not going to be defined by performance relative to the average, but by striving for the very best you could do. Sidney’s endless curiosity and the prolific, diverse body of work he produced are well known. He didn’t talk much at family gatherings about his professional success, but I remember several years before his death asking what he was working on. He’d expressed some anxiety for the need to finish a unifying perspective on mental diseases and self identity. Even after all he had achieved up to that point, he worried he did not have enough time to complete the work he wanted in his lifetime and to leave behind all the ideas he still had. He extended the high standards to which he held himself to the rest of his family. When I finished my biology thesis in college I remember him suggesting I try to get it published in Nature or Science. At the time, I remember just being grateful I had finished. After the seventh time he suggested it, I finally broke the news that I was not going to be sending anything to Nature. It was then that he explained his thinking though – the most renowned journals often give the most constructive feedback; if you start with the top the worst they can say is no, and there is always something to be gained, even just from understanding why they say no. While I had never wanted to pursue the academic research path, I think the same idea is applicable to any career – if you aim for the very top and seek the best resources you can access, you will end up going further than you could have imagined.

[[RunningHead]]

Eulogy for Sidney J. Blatt

Kay M. Long PHD

Kay M. Long

180 East Rock Road, New Haven, CT 06511
kay.long@yale.edu

Kay M. Long   Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine and a Training and Supervising Analyst at The Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis.

Sid Blatt was my teacher, mentor, and friend for over 30 years. I first met Sid when I moved from Austin to New Haven in 1986 to spend one year in the Yale predoctoral psychology training program that Sid led for almost 50 years. I never returned to Texas as I had planned, and Sid had a lot to do with that. Sid’s intellect was so vibrant that, although he died at 85, I think we were all left feeling that his life was cut short. There was something larger-than-life about Sid, be it his outsized accomplishments, his extraordinary intellect, or his voracious appetite for learning across many fields. I benefited from all of these aspects of him. But he was also a big-hearted man, which is what I carry with me most of all.

One of my earliest memories of Sid was in a course on clinical inference he taught at the Yale Psychiatric Institute. On the first day of class, Sid showed us the cover page of a patient’s chart. This form conveyed straightforward information: name, address, date of birth, date of admission, and chief complaint. It was the kind of page you would read quickly and turn over to get to the pages with the real story – the patient’s history, evaluations, case notes, and psychological testing.

We never got past that first page. Sid took that basic form and unpacked it line by line. He elaborated a series of hypotheses about the patient’s history, personality, and psychopathology based only on this bare-bones information. From the simplest data, a three-dimensional person appeared before our eyes, and a nuanced and sympathetic understanding of that person came with it. I couldn’t figure out how he had done it. It was like watching a magic show.

Sid said he would teach us how to make these kinds of clinical inferences, the psychoanalytic theories to support them, and the means to test our original hypotheses so we could have the same sensitive understanding of our patients he had just demonstrated. I was hooked. I knew then I wanted to stay in New Haven to learn as much as possible from him and, over time, from many others in this remarkable community.

[[RunningHead]]

Eulogy for Sidney J. Blatt

Diana Diamond PHD

Diana Diamond

135 Central Park West, New York, NY 10023
ddiamonda@gmail.com

Diana Diamond   Currently a Senior Fellow at the Personality Disorders Institute (PDI) at Weill Cornell Medical Center, Professor Emerita at the City University of New York, and Adjunct Full Professor at the New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis.

I first met Sid when he interviewed me for a postdoctoral fellowship at Yale. As part of my application, I had submitted a paper that linked social theory and psychoanalytic perspectives. Sid told me that he liked the paper so much he wished he had written it himself. You can imagine what it meant to me – having just completed my internship and on the cusp of deciding how seriously to take myself as a professional – to hear this from a Renaissance man in our field: a distinguished theoretician, a prolific empirical researcher, a personality theorist, and an analytic clinician who wove seamlessly among practice, theory, and research.

That first dialogue introduced me to the spirit of generosity and generativity that characterized Sid’s role as mentor, and that is what I want to focus on today. Sid recognized that a true leader trains other leaders who will carry on one’s vision while becoming themselves. That interchange was my first experience of being “panim el panim” with Sid. Panim el panim is a phrase from the Torah “denoting … a presence to another presence without an intermediary, as is said: Come let us look one another in the face.”

Relatedness and self-definition – the two lines of development so fundamental to Sid’s life and work – also guided his relationship with his students, colleagues, and collaborators. When Joan Criccia, his devoted assistant, sent me his vita after his death, I noticed that he had listed not only the names of his dissertation students, but also the names of those he had mentored over the years, a number of whom are here today. He saw his work with us as fundamental to who he was just as his mentorship of us has been fundamental to who we have become.

Panim el panim

Another transformative moment occurred when I told Sid with some trepidation that being in my mid 30s, I had to devote myself to starting a family, and therefore felt I should leave the research postdoc that followed the one-year clinical postdoc. He was very empathetic to my situation but reminded me that there are different types of creativity, and that he would not be satisfied until he saw my creativity come to fruition on several fronts, assuring me that he would adjust the postdoc to accommodate a pregnancy. He also shared his experiences of his own daughters, and his support of their decisions, sometimes to put family before work. In that dialogue, I saw what a devoted, even passionate, father and grandfather he was. Indeed, he stated that he learned about the power of the unconscious and developmental issues from being a parent and a grandparent. Sid had an extraordinary impact on the world around him, while he created an extraordinary family life for himself.

Eulogy

John Krystal MD

John Krystal

300 George Street, New Haven, CT 06510
john.krystal@yale.edu

John Krystal   Robert L. McNeil, Jr. Professor of Translational Research, Professor of Psychiatry, Neuroscience, and Psychology, Chair of the Psychiatry Department, and Co-Director of the Yale Center for Clinical Investigation at Yale University. He is also Director of the Clinical Neuroscience Division of the National Center for PTSD (VA) and the NIAAA Center on the Translational Neuroscience of Alcohol.

Hello, my name is John Krystal. I am the chair of the Yale Psychiatry Department and I have the sad task of saying goodbye, on behalf of the Department of Psychiatry and Yale University, to a man that I have known for 34 years as a teacher, scholar, healer, colleague, and friend.

Ethel, Susan, David, and Judi, please accept our deepest condolences.

Sid was an outspoken advocate for psychology and he had a huge impact on our Department. After obtaining his Ph.D. from the University of Chicago in 1957 and completing an internship with the noted psychologist, Carl Rogers, he came to Yale in 1960 and was recruited to the faculty of the Department of Psychiatry in 1963. He completed psychoanalytic training at the Western New England Psychoanalytic Institute, where he remained connected throughout his career.

For nearly 50 years, Sid led the Section of Psychology of our Department, consisting of nearly half of the 175 full-time and 400 voluntary faculty members. In this role he set high standards for clinical and academic excellence, trained generations of future leaders of psychology and psychiatry, including 40 PhD students and current Yale President Dr. Peter Salovey, and he helped to make Yale one of the world’s leading Psychiatry Departments.

What wonderful gifts Sid gave to us. Over 220 articles and 17 books, Sid wrote about the nature of the human psyche and the factors that shape our sense of our selves in relation to the people to whom we are closest.

Sid was a polymath, his writing drew on psychology, psychoanalysis, sociology, anthropology, neurobiology, genetics, developmental biology, cognitive neuroscience, and art. Sid was a scientist who brought rigorous research methods to psychoanalysis, both provoking and inspiring this field to test its most precious hypotheses.

Sid received numerous honors, too many to list today. He received the highest awards from several organizations including the American Psychological Association and American Psychoanalytic Association. Sid was the Sigmund Freud Professor at Hebrew University, the Sigmund Freud Professor; for a psychoanalyst that is like being the Isaac Newton Professor of Physics or perhaps the Sandy Koufax Professor of Pitching.

Epilogue: Internalization, Self-Other Differentiation, and Relatedness: The Enduring Legacy of Sidney J. Blatt

Kay M. Long PHD and Diana Diamond PHD

Diana Diamond

180 East Rock Road, New Haven, CT 06511
kay.long@yale.edu

135 Central Park West, New York, NY 10023
ddiamonda@gmail.com

Diana Diamond   Currently a Senior Fellow at the Personality Disorders Institute (PDI) at Weill Cornell Medical Center, Professor Emerita at the City University of New York, and Adjunct Full Professor at the New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis.

In the 10 years since Sid’s death, we have lived through many terrible threats to our safety and well-being: a world-wide pandemic which necessitated two years of lockdown, catastrophic turns in climate change that threaten our existence as we have known it, challenges to our democracy, and now the cataclysm in the Middle East. In his November 2014 eulogy Sid’s son David said: “I believe my dad’s deepest identification was his Judaism. He was neither outwardly religious nor a Jewish scholar, but he had an intimate connection to the people and land of Israel. He traveled to Israel more than a dozen times and taught at virtually every university there. Israel was his second home, both professionally and personally. Not surprisingly, his identity as a Jew was bound up in his relationship with a Jewish community.”

In keeping with the idea of face-to-face dialogue, panim al panim, we feel it is important to mention Sid’s love of righteous justice (mitzpat Tzedek). As far back as 1993, in the first Clinton administration, this love of righteous justice led Sid to be upset at the torpedoing of the nomination of Lani Guinier to be attorney general. Civil rights and human rights truly mattered to Sid. We imagine he would have extended that to Palestinians no less to Jews. As we experience these events we have carried Sid forward in our minds, reaffirming his progressive values and commitment to democracy, his dedication to the humanizing and enlightening influence of the arts and humanities, his belief that psychoanalysis is a body of knowledge that can be empirically affirmed and that will survive and flourish through a combination of theory and research. The recent development of the Department of Psychoanalytic Research (DPE) at the American Psychoanalytic Association as well as other developments in the field (Sandler research institute) are inspired by Sid’s tireless efforts in this direction.

We would be remiss if we did not highlight in closing Sid’s tremendous skill as a clinician and diagnostician and his profound dedication to his patients. Sid’s life’s work of theoretical, clinical, and empirical contributions began with a simple but profound clinical observation. During his analytic training, he saw that the two patients he was treating had similar symptoms of depression, but each was occupied with different concerns. Sid saw that his patients’ worries coalesced around two distinct but interrelated poles, what he termed self-definition and relatedness. It was a mark of his brilliance that from this observation, he developed ground-breaking theories of normal and abnormal development and personality organization, an extensive body of empirical research, and theories and techniques of therapeutic change, and he supported all of his innovative ideas with an extensive body of empirical research.

Misogyny, misogyny in psychoanalysis, transmisogyny, lgbtq, orientalism

Michaela Chamberlain deftly traces a long lineage of psychoanalytic misogyny in her recent book, Misogyny in Psychoanalysis. This review meets Chamberlain’s invitation to discuss and reflect on the varied impacts of misogyny through both a psychoanalytic and intersectional lens.

Steven H. Cooper   Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at Columbia University and an Adjunct Clinical Professor at the New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis. He is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute and the Columbia Center for Psychoanalytic Training and Research. He is Chief Editor Emeritus of Psychoanalytic Dialogues and is the author and editor of seven books in psychoanalysis. His newest two books will be published in July, 2025, Psychoanalysis in Play: Expanding Psychoanalytic Concepts from a Play Perspective and a book, Winnicott’s 1967 Letter to Bion: Beyond Playing and Dreaming that he coedited with Christopher G. Lovett.
Transference, defense, countertransference, curriculum, epistemological, ontological

Becoming a psychoanalyst has been a continuous process including clinical work, teaching, writing, and educational administration. I emphasize how I have changed in regular intervals regarding my way of thinking about clinical work, theory, and change processes within individuals and groups. In fact, psychoanalysis when it is effective embodies a process of not only examining who we are and have been, but always who we are becoming. Institutions that thrive find ways to remain curious about what is in the way of change and growth. Sources of resistance include the pulls for certainty within each of us as individuals and often exacerbated in the crucible of group contagion. First, I trace my beginnings, trying to enter an organized psychoanalysis that did not want people of my background (clinical psychologists). I highlight how much I have learned and am trying to learn about becoming a psychoanalyst in my office, teaching, editorial work, and in my writing.

Randall H. Paulsen MD

Randall H. Paulsen

415 24th Ave E, Seattle, WA 98112
rhpaulsen@mac.com

Randall H. Paulsen   Training and supervising psychoanalyst at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute, and a consulting psychoanalyst at the Seattle Psychoanalytic Society and Institute. Prior to his move from Boston to Seattle in 2022, he was an assistant professor of psychiatry at Harvard Medical School. Currently, he is a Clinical instructor in the University of Washington’s School of Medicine Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences.
Crisis, containment, leadership, boundaries, authority, responsibility, membership

A former president of the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute (BPSI) writes a memoir of his presidency. The organizational history contains personal recollections and collective responses to the several-fold crisis he inherited. The 4-year period of his presidency involved the sale of an heirloom building, the purchase of a new one, the democratic creation of a multi-level new mission statement, the management of a liquid endowment, and the design of new organizational by-laws. These efforts enabled the subsequent twenty years to be a creative and adaptive realization of the mission’s stated goals. Stages of conflict are described, and retrospective and experiential learning are provided in the hope that many of the lessons of this transformational process may be useful to other psychoanalytic and therapeutic institutes as they contend with their own change processes.

responseSet.documentInfoXML: 2025 45 6 Rainbow Reflections: Navigating the Spectrum of Experiences 501-503 Prologue: Rainbow Reflections: Navigating the Spectrum of Experiences Estelle Shane Issue Editor Distinguished psychoanalyst, educator, and author based in Los Angeles, renowned for her contributions to contemporary self psychology and relational psychoanalysis. A founding and supervising analyst at both the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis (ICP) and the New Center for Psychoanalysis (NCP), Dr. Shane also serves on the clinical faculty of the UCLA Department of Psychiatry. Her work bridges classical analytic traditions with modern understandings of trauma, attachment, and neurobiology. As a founder and past board member of the International Association for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology (IAPSP), Dr. Shane has played a pivotal role in shaping the evolution of self psychological thought. She has authored numerous influential papers and book chapters, and is co-author of Intimate Attachments: Toward a New Self Psychology. Known for her integrative clinical sensibility, Dr. Shane brings warmth, rigor, and intellectual curiosity to her teaching, supervision, and clinical practice. Her writing and teaching often center on the therapeutic relationship as a site of mutual transformation. Stacy Berlin Issue Editor Psychoanalyst and a licensed clinical psychologist practicing in Studio City, Los Angeles, California. She is on the Board of Directors of the International Forum for Psychoanalytic Education, Associate Editor of Psychoanalysis, Self and Context, and Guest Editor of Psychoanalytic Inquiry. She is a Faculty Member and Training and Supervising Analyst at the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis in Los Angeles. In her professional practice, Stacy takes an egalitarian and contextualist approach within a safe relational framework, integrating creativity, play, and humor. 4223 Vantage Avenue, Studio City, CA 91604 drstacyberlin@aol.com

In her professional practice, Stacy takes an egalitarian and contextualist approach within a safe relational framework, integrating creativity, play, and humor.

This journal issue features personal reflections from a group of highly sensitive and perceptive clinicians as they examine their own life histories alongside the theoretical and societal shifts they have observed while pursuing their unique therapeutic work. Collectively, their writings illuminate the cultural and social dynamics that have shaped their generation as they each navigate, define, and redefine their approaches to treatment, informed by continual learning.

The issue begins with an exploration of neuroscience to understand the human mind-brain-body complex, starting with traditional Freudian theory and extending to contemporary theoretical developments and technological advancements. It highlights that, despite the evolution of tools – from Freud’s couch to modern imaging techniques – the core mission to understand and navigate the self remains constant.

The issue then transitions to personal narratives from clinicians who reflect on their experiences of personal hardship and professional growth. These stories emphasize the intricate interplay between self-experiences, professional identity, and evolving practices. The articles address broader social issues, such as how societal beliefs and biases shape personal and collective consciousness, influencing individual identities and the quality of therapeutic interactions.

Moreover, our authors delve into themes like the ethics of care and the influence of personal and cultural biases in therapeutic practice. These reflections highlight the ongoing need for clinicians to self-reflect on implicit dynamics of power, identity, and culture that pervade the therapeutic space. Overall, this issue captures how each participant in the therapeutic dyad is profoundly transformed by the encounter. Below are brief discussions of the articles.

Deborah Winograd meticulously analyzes homophobia through evolutionary and neurophysiological lenses. She argues that survival instincts can foster a maladaptive and perilous proliferation of virulent, irrational hatred and violence toward vulnerable groups. These deep-seated, unconscious fears can provoke deplorable actions against groups wrongly deemed malevolent.

[[RunningHead]]

Introduction to De-Pathologizing Homosexuality: 50th Anniversary Notes on December 1973

Lois Oppenheim PHD

Lois Oppenheim

New York, NY
oppenheiml@montclair.edu

Lois Oppenheim  

On December 10, 2024, a Scientific Program was held at the New York Psychoanalytic Society and Institute entitled “Gayness and Psychoanalysis: Bias, Change.” The speaker was Lawrence Hartmann, M.D. and the discussant was Mark Smaller, Ph.D. Prior to the start of the meeting, I noted that some thirty-nine years before the American Psychiatric Association took “homosexuality” out of the DSM where it was said to be a “sociopathic personality disorder,” Freud responded to a woman in the U.S. who had written to him about the possibility of his treating her son. In his letter, Freud wrote the following: “Homosexuality […] is nothing to be ashamed of, no vice, no degradation, it cannot be classified as an illness […].” He then went on to say, “Many highly respectable individuals of ancient and modern times have been homosexuals, several of the greatest men among them (Plato, Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci, etc.). It is a great injustice to persecute homosexuality as a crime, and cruelty too.”1 Similarly, when Ernest Jones wrote the Committee about a question from the Dutch Psychoanalytical Society regarding an application for training of a homosexual psychiatrist, and he asked if advising against such acceptance, as Jones had already done, should be “a safe general maxim to act on,” Freud replied in a letter cosigned by Otto Rank, “As regards your query, dear Ernest, concerning prospective membership of homosexuals, we cannot agree with you. That is, we cannot exclude such persons in principle, for the same reasons that we also cannot condone their legal prosecution. We believe that a decision in such cases should depend on an individual examination of the other qualities of the candidate.”2 What many have long felt particularly intriguing is that pathologizing homosexuality became the norm in the American psychoanalytic establishment when Freud himself had such a different view. As intriguing are the questions of how and why change ultimately occurred. The presentation by Dr. Hartmann and discussion by Dr. Smaller did indeed shed significant light on the answers to these questions and more and for this reason we are publishing the papers presented at that NYPSI meeting.

Homosexuality, gayness, diagnosis, APA, DSM, climate around homosexuality

This paper is a brief 50th anniversary historical note. In December 1973, The American psychiatric Association, after much deliberation, removed homosexuality per se as a diagnosis from its diagnostic and statistical manual (DSM). This turned out to be an influential step in the de-pathologizing of homosexuality. This paper describes some of the climate around homosexuality before December 1973, and some contributions to that 1973 change, inside and beyond psychiatry and psychoanalysis, before and during the early 1970s. The paper also includes some notes on the workings of the APA and on the author’s participation in the change.

Deborah Robin Winograd   Clinical director of the Organizational Mind Group, PC and a psychologist in private practice in Dana Point, California. Dr. Winograd is a curriculum writer in the social neurosciences for the University of California, Davis and various other public and private organizations across the United States. She is the founder of The Mind Press, a publishing house for texts in the social neurosciences. Dr. Winograd is a field tester of continuing education books for the American Psychological Association (APA). She is also co-author of Workaches: The Neuroscience Guide to Surviving and Thriving at Work.
Homophobia, vestigial traits, psychopathology, threat, evolution, bias

Physical vestigial traits, such as wisdom teeth, are human structures that no longer serve the adaptive purpose they once did in our evolutionary past. When they erupt and become inflamed in modern society, they are typically identified as such, diagnosed and treated. Science has afforded much less attention to vestigial psychosocial or behavioral traits (emerging from neural remnants of our ancient past). There was even a lessening of Freud’s emphasis on the evolutionary nature of psychopathology early on in the post-Freudian era of psychoanalysis. This paper proposes that we investigate homophobia as a psychosocial vestigial trait that is maladaptive in contemporary society – psychopathology deserving of potential classification as such, with different subtypes, comorbidities and relevant interventions. Homosexuality was classified as psychopathology in the first edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM) in 1952—without any empirical evidence to justify its inclusion as a mental illness. Although the diagnosis was partially removed in 1973, no steps were taken to “scientifically exonerate” or to mitigate the decades of damage done by this labeling. Some fundamentalist religious ideologies and their doctrines continue to identify homosexuality as a malady and abomination. This paper proposes that this type of indoctrination infects and inflames vestigial neural structures that have been conserved from our evolutionary past. We need our “scientific bible” to counter these beliefs and to identify and research the pathology of homophobia. Science challenges harmful religious beliefs and politically motivated ideologies that have found their way into a culture’s imagination. Homophobia deserves to be viewed through a macroscopic lens as a maladaptive vestigial trait in contemporary society. Our primitive ancestors had to discriminate against those they perceived as different from their clan to enhance their survival. It was adaptive back then; it is maladaptive today. Homophobia, along with other forms of discrimination against differences, must be investigated and highlighted as psychopathological.

Conversion therapy, gay men, SOCE, trauma

Research shows that affirmative relationships and environments have a positive impact on the mental health of LGBTQIA+ people. Yet many LGBTQIA+ individuals experience relational traumas from rejecting families which may include conversion or reparative practices. This paper will discuss the unique developmental challenges LGBTQIA+ people face, the impact of early developmental stage rejection, and ways to improve clinical engagement with clients for more affirming care. From an Intersubjective Self Psychological framework, I will draw upon Daniel Shaw’s concept of relational systems of subjugation. The purpose of this paper is to raise awareness of the prevalence of conversion therapy and trauma related to religious beliefs as factors in the developmental years of LGBTQ+ people, and of the implications of this prevalence. One such implication is how political discourse and proposals of anti-LGBTQ+ policies and laws impact the mental health of LGBTQIA+ people, particularly about perceived safety. I will examine how subjugation by their caregivers/parents, communities, and other social environments toxifies LGBTQIA+ individuals’ selfobject ties and their perception of self, with far-reaching ramifications.

Koichi Togashi

Koichi Togashi   Council Member of the International Association for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology, and an Associate Editor of Psychoanalysis, Self and Context, and an Editor of Psychoanalytic Inquiry. He is an author of “Kohut’s Twinship across Cultures: The Psychology of Being Human” (co-authored with Amanda Kottler, Routledge, 2015), and “Psychoanalytic Zero: A Decolonizing Study of Therapeutic Dialogues” (Routledge, 2020).
Post-colonialism, colonizer-colonized relationship, reciprocal vulnerability, deception, Orientalism, ethical turn

When strangers encounter one another – as individuals or nations – they cannot escape finding the other’s ways and values unfamiliar and awkward. A frequent result is that they objectify and demonize the “other,” and, if they have the power, seek to “enlighten,” conquer, or destroy them. Does this same dynamic play out between therapists and patients? In this presentation, I conclude that it does, and that a colonizer-colonized relationship is created by – and creates – the essential asymmetry of the therapeutic dialogue. Through examination of two short case vignettes, I will discuss how therapists’ desire to colonize their patients (unfolding in the intersubjective field) organizes and how the colonization is organized by nonrecognition of their own vulnerability, the uncontrollability of their patients, and their primal dependency on their patients.

Homosexuality, homophobia, homophilia, visceral/moral/medical judgment

In this brief but broad-based reflection on homosexuality and gender identity as personally experienced by the author, he describes a shocking encounter with a high school friend who came out to him as gay, arousing visceral dread and revulsion for the idea of being wanted, sexually, by another man. At the same time, he was aware of the painful aloneness from which his friend was reaching out for connection and acceptance by someone he deeply respected and knew was straight. It took time and much help from both Psychoanalysis and Christianity to access and integrate the author’s feelings of love and hate, desire for and fear of his own father who died after he expressed his all-out infantile, destructive rejection. It is important, he believes, to bear not-knowing and identity-confusion to understand both homosexuality and homophobia on the way toward viable forms of homo- and hetero-philia.

Martha Stark   Faculty, Harvard Medical School; Co-Founder/Co-Director, Center for Psychoanalytic Studies, William James College; Award-winning author with nine books on the integration of psychoanalytic theory and practice; and Originator/Developer of the Psychodynamic Synergy Paradigm: A C.A.R.E.S. Approach to Deep Embodied Healing.
Difference and sameness, countertransferential blind spots, cultural introjects, othering, psychoanalytic innocence, open heart and open mind

How can we – as psychoanalytically oriented therapists – best position ourselves moment-to-moment during the actual clinical hour as we sit with our patients, whether our patients are different from us or seemingly very much the same? More specifically, how can we ever truly “know” another’s experience? Perhaps it could be said that the greatest gift we can offer our patients – and our greatest challenge – will be our ability to listen to them with open heart, open mind, and humility. Countertransferential judgments, preconceptions, and biases are constantly threatening to interfere with our ability to be fully present and compassionately engaged with our patients. It is therefore critically important that we engage in a lifelong process of self-reflection, self-critiquing, and ongoing examination of our own beliefs and identities so that we do not do patients the disserve of retreating from their vantage point.

Estelle Shane   Distinguished psychoanalyst, educator, and author based in Los Angeles, renowned for her contributions to contemporary self psychology and relational psychoanalysis. A founding and supervising analyst at both the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis (ICP) and the New Center for Psychoanalysis (NCP), Dr. Shane also serves on the clinical faculty of the UCLA Department of Psychiatry. Her work bridges classical analytic traditions with modern understandings of trauma, attachment, and neurobiology. As a founder and past board member of the International Association for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology (IAPSP), Dr. Shane has played a pivotal role in shaping the evolution of self psychological thought. She has authored numerous influential papers and book chapters, and is co-author of Intimate Attachments: Toward a New Self Psychology. Known for her integrative clinical sensibility, Dr. Shane brings warmth, rigor, and intellectual curiosity to her teaching, supervision, and clinical practice. Her writing and teaching often center on the therapeutic relationship as a site of mutual transformation.

As we imagine you have seen for yourselves, the contributions in this issue encapsulate a broad exploration of four overarching themes: First, the evolution of identity for both patients and clinicians; Second, the influence of personal experiences on professional practice, both overt and unconscious; Third, the existence of power dynamics within psychoanalytic treatment, also both overt and unconscious; Fourth, the ongoing challenge of recognizing and addressing societal biases within the broader therapeutic context.

Many of the individual articles here share specific themes. For example, Winograd, Stark, and Santo’s articles illustrate clinicians actively navigating the change process of their identities more directly through self-experience. Nelson Warner also demonstrates how self-awareness continually shapes and enriches her practice discussing the evolution of her personal and professional identity, explaining how identities evolve through experience and interaction in and out of the consulting room. They are not static, then, but emerge through relationships with important others.

Articles highlighting the power dynamics inherent in therapy emphasize that clinicians must be aware of their potential outsized influence on patients. They must carefully balance both guiding their patients and respecting their patients’ autonomy. Togashi describes the “colonizer-colonized” dynamics present in treatment, and Sloane emphasizes the considerations necessary for maintaining ethical therapeutic relationships while at the same time remaining cautious of reproducing power structures. Winograd reveals her need to reframe her own biases in an effort to help her patient maintain pride in her own good intentions as she acted, more or less successfully, to guide her grandson’s development.

The issue also offers a synthesis of profound psychological explorations, particularly concerning identity and therapeutic engagement. Each contributor provides unique insights into personal and professional growth within the therapeutic context. Winograd highlights her ongoing pursuit to understand the human psyche, advocating for integrating neuroscience and evolutionary psychology into psychoanalytic understanding. Nelson Warner emphasizes the fluidity of identity and clinical practice shaped by diverse influences. Santo illustrates therapeutic challenges and breakthroughs in dealing with sexual identity issues that may surround religious thought and practice. Togashi examines the ethical implications of therapeutic and personal biases. Sloane shares insights on LGBTQ+ issues and on confronting problematic preconceptions. Stark discusses the critical role of empathy and cultural sensitivity in therapy.

Mariana Velykodna PHD and Oksana Yakushko PHD ABPP

Office 303, Heroiv ATO Street, 79, Kryvyi Rih 50086, Ukraine

Oksana Yakushko   Psychologist, psychoanalyst, scholar and consultant based in Santa Barbara, California, USA. She is a member of Ukrainian Diaspora in the U.S., and has been engaged in writing about and working with Ukrainians (both in Ukraine, the US, and abroad) since start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. She has taught at various academic institutions, and is an author of two books as well as numerous articles and book chapters. Starting in the Summer 2024, she will serve as the Director of the doctoral psychology program at George Washington University, Washington D.C., USA. Her work has received numerous awards, including the 2023 Research Award by the Division 39, Society for Psychoanalytic Psychology, APA and the 2023 International Leadership award by the Division 52, Society for International Psychology, APA. She is a Fellow of the American Psychological Association, and has served as on the editorial board of several scholarly journals, including the newly established Ukrainian Psychoanalytic Journal.

The history of psychoanalysis shows that Ukraine has been central to its development from the early beginning (Nalyvaiko, 2023). The fact that Freud’s family originally comes from the small west-Ukrainian towns – Tysmenytsia and Brody – holds pride for many Ukrainians (Romanov & Pushkareva, 2000). In addition, one of Freud’s most famous and long-term patients, often mistakenly considered Russian – Sergei Pankejeff – lived in the Ukrainian city of Odesa (Freud, 1914/2010). As early as 1904 (13 years before the Soviet revolution in 1917), it was Ukraine-based psychoanalysts who carried out the first translations of Freud’s works from German and authored their own papers using psychoanalytic thinking (Butsykin, 2023). Psychoanalytic groups in Odesa, Kharkiv and Kyiv were active, and there were numerous psychoanalytic communities at that time (Nalyvaiko, 2023; Romanov & Pushkareva, 2000). In 1914, Freud himself claimed that the only well-trained early psychoanalyst lived and practiced in Odesa, Ukraine, which was under Russian imperial rule then – Mosche Wulff (Freud, 1914), who completed his training analysis in Berlin with Karl Abraham (Savchenko, 2021).

After the Bolshevik revolution of 1917, which led to the formation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR) in 1922, Ukraine, along with several other non-Russian nation-states, was falsely promised independence and “equality” in exchange for joining the Soviet alliance. Under Soviet rule, psychoanalysis initially received great support from the Moscow-based Russian government because several key leaders, such as Lev Trotsky, expressed interest in psychoanalysis (Miller, 1986). The early Bolshevik policy on psychoanalysis permitted the creation of psychoanalytic institutions across territories that the Bolsheviks controlled. However, these Soviet psychoanalysts were required to submit to a single state goal, guiding their scholarship or practice – to utilize the psychoanalytic knowledge toward a purposeful “formation” of an ideal Soviet personality or a “Soviet man” (Etkind, 2013). Such an ideal person, the Soviet government stressed, was shaped from their early childhood. Thus, Soviet children became a distinct target for “pedagogical” and psychoanalytic “experiments” often held in orphanages or similar “educational” institutions, where Soviet-born infants and children were separated from their parents for purposes of Soviet reeducation (Hai et al., 2020; Nelin, 2021). However, after the Soviet authorities discovered that psychoanalysis failed to “form” and train such an ideal Soviet person or exert full ideological control over children and adults, psychoanalysis was declared to be socially dangerous. Bolshevik leaders like Lev Trotsky were demoted from their status of great revolutionary heroes and declared to be the “enemy of the people” (most were then executed, sent to Gulags, or, as in the case of Trotsky, assassinated by Russo-Soviet authorities). Even the word “psychoanalysis” in the USSR was replaced with the term “Freudo-Trotskyism” and declared to be problematically bourgeois and “Western” (Dukes, 2002). Psychoanalysis was fully banned as an anti-Soviet, anti-socialist, and anti-communist practice by the Stalinist government in 1932 (Angelini, 2008).

Mariana Velykodna   Psychological Sciences, is a Clinical Psychologist, EuroPsy registered psychologist, and a certified Psychoanalytic Practitioner of the European Confederation of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapies. She works as a Head of the Psychoanalytic Psychology and Psychotherapy Division of the National Psychological Association of Ukraine, an Associate Professor of the Practical Psychology Department at Kryvyi Rih State Pedagogical University (Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine), an Associate Professor of the Psychology Department at Ukraine Sigmund Freud University (Kyiv, Ukraine), an Editor-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Psychoanalytic Journal, and a Psychoanalyst in private practice (Kyiv, Ukraine). She is an IRC 2023-2024 Scholar Award Winner at Division 39 (Society for Psychoanalysis and Psychoanalytic Psychology) of the American Psychological Association.
Psychoanalytic psychotherapy, psychoanalysis, 2022 Russian invasion, thinking, Ukraine, war

This paper presents the author’s considerations of how Russia’s war against Ukraine impacted the ability to think and the capacity to empathize among psychoanalytically oriented practitioners. She first describes and discusses the observed patterns among external psychoanalytic responses to the 2022 Russian invasion of Ukraine. Secondly, she reflects on these patterns through the prism of her own reactions to the 2014 Russian invasion of Eastern Ukraine and the Crimea annexation. Lastly, she offers her considerations about the limits and possibilities of psychoanalytic thinking, practice, and training in the context of wars. Overall, the author proposes associating the psychic responses to war with (a) the war mode of psychic functioning and related defenses against it, (b) psychoanalytically informed propaganda influence, and (c) peculiarities of psychoanalytic training and practice, which set a specific type of thinking.

Military psychology, Narcissism, psychoanalysis, Russian invasion, self, war

The paper highlights the psychoanalytic approach to understanding the state of the Self-system among military personnel who were directly involved in combat operations as a result of the Russian Federation’s attack on Ukraine. Using the Narcissism Inventory, the author presents the results of an empirical study of 83 soldiers during their treatment and rehabilitation and provides three clinical case vignettes to illustrate and discuss these findings. The author discusses the revealed specifics of the Self-system functioning of the Ukrainian military in response to direct combat and physical injuries through a psychoanalytic lens.

Valeriy Dorozhkin   Psychological Sciences, is a Psychologist, EuroPsy registered psychologist, member of the Psychoanalytic Psychology and Psychotherapy Division of the National Psychological Association of Ukraine, a certified Balint groups leader, Psychodynamic psychotherapist in private practice (Kyiv, Ukraine), and a Professor of Theoretical and Practical Psychology Department at Lviv Polytechnic National University (Lviv, Ukraine).
War, psychoanalysis, Russian invasion, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, trauma, Ukraine

“Psychologists during War” is one of the numerous social projects conducted in Ukraine following the Russian armed invasion. The project united psychoanalysts, psychotherapists, and crisis psychologists who were providing assistance to Ukrainians since the first days of the Russian occupational invasion. The analysis of this project illustrates the evolution of the understanding of crisis and psychotherapeutic first aid, the dynamics and changes of processes in society following a social catastrophe, as well as psychological patterns and work conditions in liberated regions and areas close to the frontline. The article discusses mental phenomena, such as intersubjective and intrasubjective processes, caused by the invasion. The article provides insights into socio-psychological phenomena and peculiarities of the analytic work during the protracted war. The article investigates the influences of mental states on social processes and vice versa within Ukrainian society.

This letter was written by a psychoanalyst from Dnipro, Ukraine, who serves as a deputy battalion commander for moral and psychological support and as a captain in the Armed Forces of Ukraine since the 2022 Russian invasion. In this contribution, which was based on the oral presentation at the conference of the International Psychoanalytical Studies Organization in Uzhhorod, Ukraine (December 2023), he speaks on the (im)possibility of psychoanalysis during the war, referring to his own considerations, psychoanalytic papers, literature, and art.

He was the first President of the Ukrainian Psychoanalytic Society, which is a study group of the IPA.
Therapeutic dyad, psychoanalysis, setting, 2022 Russian invasion, Ukraine

This contribution describes psychoanalytic work during an extreme situation of war. The impact of war conditions on patients’ functioning and the process of psychoanalytic engagement with them is examined. Specifically, this work stresses the impact of the attacks on the setting and changes in the structure of relations. The author further reflects on challenges to preservation of the analytic process under the conditions of breached confidentiality as well as possible ways to address the challenges of war to the psychoanalytic professional identity. The article is an attempt to understand how psychoanalysts could maintain the psychoanalytic container or their analytic self in catastrophic situations, which intend to destroy both settings and people.

Oksana Yakushko PHD ABPP

Oksana Yakushko

123 W. Padre Street, Suite C, Santa Barbara, CA 93105
oyakushko@gmail.com

Oksana Yakushko   Psychologist, psychoanalyst, scholar and consultant based in Santa Barbara, California, USA. She is a member of Ukrainian Diaspora in the U.S., and has been engaged in writing about and working with Ukrainians (both in Ukraine, the US, and abroad) since start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. She has taught at various academic institutions, and is an author of two books as well as numerous articles and book chapters. Starting in the Summer 2024, she will serve as the Director of the doctoral psychology program at George Washington University, Washington D.C., USA. Her work has received numerous awards, including the 2023 Research Award by the Division 39, Society for Psychoanalytic Psychology, APA and the 2023 International Leadership award by the Division 52, Society for International Psychology, APA. She is a Fellow of the American Psychological Association, and has served as on the editorial board of several scholarly journals, including the newly established Ukrainian Psychoanalytic Journal.
War, Russian imperialism, Freud, Dostoyevsky, Russophilia

Russophilia, or the valoration of the supposed “greatness” and superiority of Russian culture and politics, especially paralleled with purposeful erasure of its engagement in violent ideologies and acts, has been present in “Western” (i.e. external to Russia) accounts, including in psychoanalysis. Psychoanalytic contributions on Fyodor Dostoyevsky as a “great” literary and allegedly psychologically salubrious figure are illustrative of this tendency. Russophilic filters are evident in how and what works by Dostoyevsky are read in psychoanalysis while Freud’s original appraisals of Dostoyevsky’s social and political sadism are minimized or expunged. These Russophilic tendencies in relation to Dostoyevsky parallel similar processes of continued promotion of Russian and Soviet imperialism, which are used to rationalize current Russian aggression toward Ukraine, including among psychoanalytic intellectuals. This contribution conceptualizes these trends via psychoanalytic theories on group psychology and social defenses against realities of cultural-political sadism, totalitarianism, and ideological intellectualizing.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue: Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy in Wartime: Ukraine — (Not) Bearing the War: Psychoanalytic Reflections on the Russian Invasion of Ukraine

Oksana Yakushko PHD ABPP and Mariana Velykodna PHD

Mariana Velykodna

4th floor, Klovskyi uzviz, 7, Kyiv 01021, Ukraine
velykodna@kdpu.edu.ua

Mariana Velykodna   Ph.D. in Psychological Sciences, is a Clinical Psychologist, EuroPsy registered psychologist, and a certified Psychoanalytic Practitioner of the European Confederation of Psychoanalytic Psychotherapies. She works as a Head of the Psychoanalytic Psychology and Psychotherapy Division of the National Psychological Association of Ukraine, an Associate Professor of the Practical Psychology Department at Kryvyi Rih State Pedagogical University (Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine), an Associate Professor of the Psychology Department at Ukraine Sigmund Freud University (Kyiv, Ukraine), an Editor-in-Chief of the Ukrainian Psychoanalytic Journal, and a Psychoanalyst in private practice (Kyiv, Ukraine). She is an IRC 2023-2024 Scholar Award Winner at Division 39 (Society for Psychoanalysis and Psychoanalytic Psychology) of the American Psychological Association.

We are writing this epilogue during the days of some of the most horrific Russian attacks on Ukraine: In the holiday period, between December 29th, 2023, and January 2nd, 2024, the Russian president authorized the Russian military to send nearly 100 deadly guided precision missiles and drones, murdering and maiming civilians while destroying homes, schools, hospitals, museums. … Meanwhile, Russian president Putin’s celebratory speeches continue with the propaganda that the murder of Ukrainians is Russia’s “existential self-defense” against the threats and evil of the “West.” Militarized brutality toward Ukraine and Ukrainians continues since the full-scale invasion in February 2022, but the “special military operation” to “de-Nazify” Ukraine and to “protect the Russian-speaking minorities” was shown as nothing but a vicious imperialist grab. Both Putin and his Russophilic mouthpieces, who are found (unfortunately) even in the psychoanalytic community, continue their rhetoric that murder, torture, destruction, ecocide, linguicide, and genocide committed against Ukrainians are justified for ideological reasons when they are packaged for whatever ideological commitment that suits those who rationalize violence (e.g., Ukraine is a colony, it does not exist outside of “Russia,” or Ukraine is a NATO wielding threat, or “peace” requires Ukrainians to submit to occupation).

Meanwhile, Ukrainian analysts, whose works were included in this contribution, continue their work on the frontlines, in hospitals with wounded, in their offices, online, and in their professional community. In this contribution, Velykodna analyzes the psychic responses to war, which highlight how both individual and social defenses, at times endemic in psychoanalytic types of thinking, can lead to difficulties with acknowledging and emotionally engaging with wars and those who are impacted by them. Pustovoyt discusses his psychoanalytic work with wounded Ukrainian defenders through direct empirical observations and case studies, showing that varied psychic self-systems can be engaged among physically injured individuals who serve in the military against Russian aggression. Dorozhkin documented the work of the entire psychoanalytic project, involving numerous psychoanalytic clinicians, in community-based efforts to work with individuals and groups of Ukrainians who survived physically and psychologically torturous Russian occupation. Fedorets discusses ways in which psychoanalytic work is significantly and profoundly changed under conditions of war violence, noting that survival of catastrophic crises and life-threatening conditions shapes all aspects of a psychoanalytic encounter. Offering four markable clinical illustrations, Lagutin thoroughly analyzes the difficulties of preserving the familiar relationships of a psychoanalytic dyad in the context of the ongoing intrusion of war into the analytic space. The letter from the front by a psychoanalyst who is serving in the Ukrainian defense forces, Garmish, directly holds the possibilities and impossibilities of psychoanalytic work and, most important, remaining human and relating under conditions of surviving the aggression in the trenches of war.

[[RunningHead]]

When the Play Stops: Transformations in Child Treatment

Amy Joelson LCSW

Amy Joelson

One Christopher Street, Suite 1A, New York, NY 10014
amy.joelson@gmail.com

Amy Joelson   Faculty and Director of Distance Learning at the Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity in NYC; President of the International Association for Psychoanalytic Self Psychology; Associate Faculty at the Japanese Forum of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology in Hiroshima, Japan; Member of IARPP’s Child, Adolescent and Parent Psychotherapy Committee; and in private practice in NYC in adult, child and adolescent treatment. Research interests include intersubjective nonlinear dynamic systems and other theories of development as applied to the analytic process.
Intersubjective systems, development, play, child treatment, pandemic, agency

The capacity for playing together came into question when my treatment of 8-year-old Chloe moved to Zoom. It was the start of the pandemic. What happened to our play? How would the disruption of Chloe’s familiar way of being in the world, including our familiar way of going-on-playing together, impact her development? This paper demonstrates that challenges do not stop development; rather they inspire new strategies. Using an intersubjective systems approach, this paper furthers ideas about playing and about development. It explores what may be transpiring between analyst and patient when the play is thwarted; and it illustrates how new vital developmental pathways are cocreated even under dire circumstances. While the process described is specific to one dyad in the context of the pandemic lockdown, the underlying understandings of social matrix and individual development are applicable at any age, to treatments with children and adults alike.
