Psychotherapy Intervention to Overcome the Difficulty of the “Possibility of Coexistence” Manifested by the COVID-19 Pandemic

Shinichi Yoshizawa PHD

Shinichi Yoshizawa

4-4-8 Yoga, Setagaya-Ku, Tokyo 158-0097, Japan
shinichiyoshizawa001@gmail.com

Shinichi Yoshizawa   Affiliated with the Family Mental Clinic Matsutani, and Member of “Support Agency for Child Psychotherapy” – Japan. Interests include impasses in psychoanalytic psychotherapy treatment of traumatized children and adults, and the recovery and development of therapist functioning. Recent publication: Editor, Becoming a Psychoanalytic Therapist for Children: Narratives of Emotional Experiences in Practice and Training (2021).
COVID-19, child psychotherapy, coexistence, countertransference, mother–child relationship

This study aimed to examine how individual-level problems faced by children with vulnerable sense of self interacted with social-level problems during the COVID-19 pandemic, focusing on the difficulty of achieving coexistence. The clinical material presents interactions with a 10-year-old boy who was not attending school and displayed violent behavior. In addition, he faced challenges regarding the intergenerational transmission of the theme concerning what has been prevalent in the family culture. The outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic led to an increase in anxiety and fear at the societal level, presence of different variants of viruses, and difficulties in coexisting with others. Individual-level problems of coexistence, which were difficult to address in regular psychotherapy, became more complex owing to the overlapping effects of social-level problems. The therapist faced the difficulty of working with the countertransference of two mixed emotional experiences: the infection caused by an invisible virus and the infection of primitive emotions in the child’s infantile part through projective identification. In working on this countertransference, it was important for the therapist to hold on to his own experiences of coexistence to maintain his function as a therapist. Furthermore, the search for how the therapist and child could coexist in psychotherapy led to a “consensus process,” leading to an equal relationship. Based on such internal work of the therapist and the “consensus process,” the child’s vulnerable boundaries were modified, and an adequate multilayered boundary became established, which generated the “possibility of coexistence.”

Paige LaCava PHD LCPC

Paige LaCava

1609 Sherman Avenue, #314, Evanston, IL 60201

Paige LaCava   Psychotherapist in private practice in Evanston, Illinois. She has a Master’s in Counseling Psychology from Northwestern University, a Certificate in Adult Psychotherapy from the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis, and is a Certified Group Psychotherapist. Interests include: the young adult, the experience of ‘launching’ in family life, and parenting. She is a Consulting Editor for Psychoanalytic Inquiry and a Council Member, International Association of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology.
Zoom psychotherapy, adolescent, microprocessing, empathy, mentalizing, affect regulation

In the suddenness of Covid lockdown and months of quarantine that followed, all of social life worldwide transitioned to Zoom. People were suffering, and yet the idea of initiating new treatments online felt disorienting to many therapists because it was new and they too were facing personal challenges during the pandemic. Like pilots in an emergency must fly without a horizon line, maneuvering their planes based on intuition and skill, those therapists who did initiate online treatments during early Covid had to suspend their usual rituals of becoming acquainted and try to connect without familiar knowns such as consulting rooms and shared space. I found working with this teen even more complicated because she refused the camera from the first session. With few visual cues, I had to sense meanings, attuning to my own body and associations, then use those loosely held reflections, combined with her more apparent responses as we navigated our work together.

Jackie Gotthold

Jackie teaches and presents at psychoanalytic conferences and institutes globally. Jackie is a member of IAPSP, and IARPP. Making sense of experience is our pan-theoretical mission. What happens when we all become a bit unmoored and a few moments run into weeks and weeks? What happens to even the “best analyzed” when fears and anxieties prevail over disorder, chaos, and uncertainty.

In the United States, as well as, much of the rest of the world, that sanctity of psychotherapeutic space – the consultation room; that privately co-created dyadic world of patient and therapist, and that “specialness” of our co-configured ways of doing things together (Lyons-Ruth et al., 1998), vanished in March 2020 – in what felt like an instant. Elsewhere, other countries had differing time frames and gradations of interventions. Still, lockdowns, social distancing, remote learning, and telehealth have become part of the global pandemic lexicon.

This issue presents the work of talented and creative child and adolescent therapists. Their respective clinical processes demonstrate a disciplined, pan-theoretical engagement with their patients. The writer’s desire and intent to connect and “accompany” their patients during a time of crisis and chaos is palpable. Notably, the therapist’s work with Riku, Chloe, and Gemma elucidated a committed bidirectional stance, where a Systems understanding of the clinical relationship comes to the fore. In all the case material presented, a relentless application of bidirectional is reflective in the relationships between child and adolescent patients and their analysts. In each case, we “hear” and can observe the dyad’s “conspiring” and “compromising” to sustain their relationships in the face of disruptions from COVID-19, governmental restrictions, and technological limitations.

“Psychotherapy” – a safe, confidential time with one’s therapist, a privileged and almost luxurious process, became a demand of one more hour on the screen. For children and adolescents in treatment, in particular, already “on-screen” in school 2–6 h a day, while maintaining connections with friends and family on screen, the added treatment hour could be “brutal.” Seemingly, unbridgeable changes were occurring for psychoanalysis and psychotherapy.

On Being and Becoming a Psychoanalyst Director

Catherine Rising Kimble MD

Catherine Rising Kimble

9 Meriam Street, Lexington, MA 02420
catherinekimblemd@gmail.com

Catherine Rising Kimble   Psychoanalyst Executive Director and Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Society, and Institute; Supervisor, MGH-McLean Psychiatry Residency Training Program; and Co-Director, MGH-McLean Program in Psychodynamics (PiP).
Psychoanalytic education, projection, consensus, transference, leadership, organizational change

A new position of Psychoanalyst Director was created at The Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute (BPSI), at a time of turmoil that catalyzed a period of organizational growth and change. I describe aspects of being a Director through the lens of my experience as the first psychoanalyst to hold the position at BPSI. I focus on a formative time before the role was created, where I learned the foundations of a Director role and ways of helping a psychoanalytic group change, move through polarizations to develop consensus, and work creatively. I then describe aspects of being a Director, including working as part of a leadership team, learning to be a transference figure, and serving the work of psychoanalytic education as an internal consultant. I highlight ways of leading that helped create an effective psychoanalytic organization focused on rigorous education, new initiatives, and a culture of psychoanalytic generativity.

When we first decided to create a Psychoanalytic Inquiry issue centered on the LGBTQ+, we weren’t sure how the broader psychoanalytic field would respond. To our delight, the response from colleagues – both known and new – was overwhelmingly enthusiastic. The sheer volume of interest quickly made it clear that this topic could not be addressed adequately in a single issue. We organized the submissions into three overarching themes, beginning with an issue on Gay Life and we are now thrilled to present the second issue, dedicated to transgender experiences.

The essays gathered in this issue traverse the evolving terrain of gender as it is lived, imagined, embodied, and encountered in psychoanalytic practice. As analysts increasingly engage with transgender, nonbinary, and gender-expansive patients, these contributions refuse closure – of identity, of meaning, or of the analytic process. Instead, they remain attuned to the unconscious as it intersects with the lived complexity of gendered life.

Gender, in these pages, is not a static identity to be affirmed or denied, but a space of becoming. Across childhood and parenthood, trauma and transition, silence and speech, gender emerges in relation – to others, to culture, to the analyst. These writers listen for longing and defense, and for the process of inhabiting a gendered world.

Throughout these authors there is a shared conviction: analytic listening must evolve, and the frame must stretch. The analyst’s own positionality – gendered, racialized, situated – cannot be disavowed. Drawing from clinical work and interdisciplinary thought, these authors offer a psychoanalysis that is ethically engaged, politically aware, and alive.

We open this issue with a wide-ranging conversation between psychoanalysts and coauthors Ann Pellegrini and Avgi Saketopoulou, whose book Gender Without Identity has already made waves. Interviewed by us – Stacy Berlin and Estelle Shane – this conversation is not merely a reflection but a provocation. With clarity and intensity, Pellegrini and Saketopoulou explore the ethical stakes of contemporary analytic work amidst political backlash and cultural confusion.

Transness, surrender, gender fluidity, enigma, interdisciplinarity

In this wide-ranging and generative conversation, Ann Pellegrini and Avgi Saketopoulou reflect on the origins of their collaboration and the theoretical, clinical, and political commitments that shaped their coauthored book Gender Without Identity. Tracing their distinct yet converging paths – from academic, activist, and clinical spaces – they explore how transness is often misunderstood, pathologized, or contained within psychoanalytic discourse, and argue instead for an expansive, ethically grounded psychoanalysis that embraces gender variability as fundamental rather than exceptional. Drawing on Laplanche, Ghent, Bromberg, and Glissant, among others, the discussion spans questions of surrender, libidinal life, intergenerational trauma, and the reorganization of theory itself under the pressure of gender. They challenge binaries between sexuality and gender, activism and analysis, clinical neutrality and sociopolitical complicity, making a case for theory as a living practice responsive to trans lives and the unconscious alike. They both offer not only insight into their thinking but also a model of interdisciplinary dialogue – one in which curiosity animates the work of rethinking psychoanalysis from the inside out. Rethinking psychoanalysis, not in spite of transness, but through it.

His upcoming books are Gender with Sexuality; situations of psychoanalytic learning and Gender: A Contemporary Introduction (both published by Routledge).
Gender, transitioning, affirmation, ethics, negative capabilities, autonomy

There are now deep debates within psychoanalytics regarding approaches of care for an adolescent presenting as non-binary or transgender. These debates are vastly split. While some view the child’s demand to transition as a matter of self-knowledge that calls for “affirmation,” others raise concerns over the child or adolescent’s capacity to discern between “need and wish” and warn against affirmation of a young person’s gendered assertions. In this paper, I focus on the question of care through a close reading of Eve Watson paper “Transitioning and Variance in Children and Adolescents: Some Temporal and Ethical Considerations.” Watson’s robust critique of the affirmative model and the “watchful waiting model” centers on a number of ethical concerns that bear on the question of the child and adolescent’s desire and its saturation. Her critique, however, leaves us with a question. What do we imagine affirmation to be? I use Watson’s critique of affirmations to address the instabilities of the term and its implication in considering the clinical encounter with the trans child.

Pain eviscerates my soul

like a knife that plunges

to unknown depths,

so little provokes those

unpredictable triggers.

I gasp, my breath is stolen.

I am betrayed. Blood

oozes from the wound.

Pressure-hold upon the gash

This issue argues that gender, in its many expressions, is not a static identity to be affirmed or a developmental error to be corrected. It is a movement – through language, body, memory, and relation – that both unsettle and extend psychoanalysis. We witness the analytic pair confronting questions that resist resolution: How does one stay present to dissociation without retraumatizing? How does one affirm without foreclosing? How do we navigate the tension between our theories and our patients’ lived needs and demands for recognition and survival?

These pieces do not offer singular answers but cultivate a shared ethic: to make room for gender not as a problem to be solved, but as a phenomenon that shapes – and is shaped by – the analytic encounter. They model a psychoanalysis that risks unknown territory that bears with the opacity of another’s becoming, and that registers the social and historical forces that live in our consulting rooms. Since gender is mediated by fantasy, history, and desire, we mostly work to make it livable.

Ann Pellegrini and Avgi Saketopoulou offer an aperture in the echo chamber of psychoanalysis, dialogue emerging from the very sites where identity has too often been presumed, policed, or pathologized. What they present is not a tidy conclusion, but a shared becoming: a rigorous surrender to the complexity of gender, theory, and the unconscious as sites of continual emergence. They speak not merely of transness, but through it – as a lens, a method, and a vital disruption that psychoanalysis can no longer afford to dismiss, domesticate, or defer.

Their conversation with us, Stacy Berlin and Estelle Shane, holds both tenderness and torque. They do not argue for a place at the analytic table but for a reconstitution of the table itself, one capacious enough to hold contradiction, opacity, ambivalence, and the risks of clinical encounter. The name, body, and the analyst’s own gender are all invited to the shifiting playing field.

They resist the choice between affirmation and pathology and stake a claim on theory as a form of care, and care as an act of imagination. What emerges is not agreement but attunement, not a fixed identity, but a becoming. They model what it means to co-theorize across difference – not to dissolve it, but to be animated by it. The psychoanalysis they call for: holds fear of the unknown, pleasure of unfixing, and ethics of listening without foreclosure.

She is a certified hypnotherapist and an EMDR-trained practitioner. Transgender embodiment, traumatophilia, eating disorders, dissociative process, dreaming, mourning

Clinical stories comprise gaps, missing pieces, and unknowable elements. In this paper, I revisit treatment with a transgender female patient through a traumatophilic and gender-expansive lens. Body dysmorphia and bulimarexic symptoms express the patient’s longing for a feminized body shape and size, the sequelae of her tortured relationship with her transgender body. Addressing her disordered eating and the underlying affect regulatory dimensions of her behavior are vital features of our analytic work. The patient’s traumatic experience, in the present, is viewed as a necessary living through her under-symbolized traumatic past, now a shareable event in our therapeutic relationship. However, questions linger about the patient’s underlying dissociative processes that needed deeper engagement. I argue that clinical writing creates space for reflection and mourning as therapeutic endeavors often leave much unsaid, unresolved, and unhealed in the patient, the analyst, and the therapeutic dyad.

I am writing this in mid-2024 as the United States elections loom and authoritarianism is a growing global threat. The “anti-gender ideology movement” in Russia, the Vatican, Italy, Brazil, Taiwan, England, and other parts of the world characterizes gender as the most destructive force in the world and a monolithic threat to children, national security, masculinity, and the differences between the sexes. In Who’s Afraid of Gender (2024), Judith Butler points out that there are many reasons to fear: climate change, forced migration, war, capitalism and neoliberal economic policies that deprive people of basic necessities, misogyny, the rollback of reproductive freedoms, and systemic racism. QTBIPOC and women “are murdered at appalling rates” (p. 5).

In this setting of annihilation anxiety, anti-gender advocates have turned gender into a “phantasmatic scene” where “intimate fears and anxieties become socially organized to incite political passions” (Butler, 2024, p. 9) and “hatred is stoked and rationalized by moral righteousness” (Butler, 2024, p. 11). In an attempt to understand this anti-gender phantasmatic scene, Butler uses dream theory and the ideas of Jean Laplanche:

For when the scene is set, and something called gender is imagined to be acting on children or affecting the public in nefarious and destructive ways, “gender” substitutes for a complex set of anxieties and becomes an overdetermined site where the fear ofdestruction gathers. (2024, p. 10)

This authoritarian campaign of projection and reversal, used to deny the rights and the existence of others, raises the questions, “Who is out to destroy whom? And how do forms of shared and escalating moral sadism pass themselves off as a virtuous order?” (Butler, 2024, p. 11).

The articles in this issue elaborate a multiplicity of queer perspectives on psychoanalysis. All the authors value the radical possibilities of psychoanalysis, even in the face of hostility and hatred within psychoanalysis and the larger culture. There is a sense of doom in the British High Court case, Bell v. Tavistock, in the terrifying effects of “charitable hatred,” and in trans-exclusionary radical feminism. Conversely, there is a sense of freedom and possibility in queer dance, queer parenting, and queer autotheory. The articles provide us with varied models of integration of queerness through historical paradigms, a theory of shared Otherness, a theory of archetypes, and by using show tunes. All the authors reach out to us and ask, as Murad Khan does so brilliantly, “Aaja Nachle—come, let’s dance!

Classical psychoanalysis has had a long, problematic history in relation to working with substance use. It wasn’t long ago that the narcissist was deemed un-analyzable and excluded from psychoanalytic treatment, as was the alcoholic or substance user until they were able to achieve and maintain sobriety. Very few analysts treated the active substance user; many still don’t. If and when they did, their attitude toward their patient was too often one of disdain and resignation, an unfortunate legacy of their ingrained sense that the substance user was an incorrigible “nuisance” (White, 1998). Although early theorists did offer many useful theories about the etiology of alcoholism and substance use (Freud, 1905/1953; Kohut, 1977/1994; Krystal & Raskin, 1970; Wurmser, 1974), the available interventions at the time were clinically irrelevant. The substance user experienced the scientific objectivism of the analyst as emotionally mis-attuned, even injurious. In addition, the interpretation of transference, the provision of insight, and the mandate to renounce childish behaviors – consistent with the idea of repudiating one’s instinctual life – were interventions that activated powerful transferences of resentment and defiance for many patients. These dynamics would not only lead to interruptions of these treatments but would also put the substance user at a greater risk for relapse. The deep tragedy here is that the failure of these therapies was quite often blamed on the patient, and their broadly defined “resistances” were the explanation given for the ineffectiveness of what we understand today as a mismatched therapeutic approach and the absence of attuned responsiveness on the part of the therapist.

Over many decades, the traditional addiction field and the tenets of Alcoholics Anonymous have reinforced these problematic assumptions about the character of the alcoholic and substance user (Jones, 2009). These treatments are most often uniformly reductionistic as they have generally understood addictive action through the teleological lens and bottom lines of genetic endowment and “disease.” These therapeutic approaches focus on treating symptoms, and, as a result, cannot avoid becoming “one size fits all” endeavors that tend to obscure the human context and preclude a deeper understanding of the emotional complexities of the substance-using patient.

Addiction, compulsion, helplessness, narcissistic rage

Addictions are psychological symptoms, a subset of compulsions. Because addictions are sometimes focused on drugs, observers for millennia have made the mistake of thinking that drugs and their effects are relevant to the nature of this psychological mechanism. Addictions, like other common symptoms, are also not linked to any one character type or level of psychological development. Understanding the psychology at work in addiction allows for its proper treatment and is best practiced by people with a psychodynamic/psychoanalytic understanding of human behavior.

Intersubjective Self Psychology, leading edge, trailing edge, ATM, generative transference

This article takes an in-depth view of addiction and its’ treatment through the lens of Intersubjective Self Psychology (ISP) and amalgamates ISP’s focus on the trailing and leading edges with the self psychological theory and treatment approach to addiction proposed by Richard Ulman and myself in The Self Psychology of Addiction and Its Treatment: Narcissus in Wonderland (2006). ISP and Narcissus both regard a shared unconscious narcissistic fantasy in the form of selfobject experiences to be at the heart of the treatment process. ISP expands these ideas and, in particular, offers a more complete understanding of the treatment of addiction, first with a focus on the analysis of the trailing and leading edges of both participants in the intersubjective field and then how the unfolding leading edge is the facilitator of psychological growth.

A Convergence of Treatments and Ideas: Psychoanalysis Meets Harm Reduction Therapy

Debra Rothschild PHD

Debra Rothschild

30 West 70th Street, #1C, New York, NY 10023
deberoth@gmail.com

Debra Rothschild   New York State-licensed psychologist, certified psychoanalyst and substance use therapist in private practice in New York City. She is faculty, supervisor and graduate of the New York University Postdoctoral Program in Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis and a supervisor at the National Institute for the Psychotherapies (NIP) in New York as well as the City College of New York Clinical Psychology program. Debra is on the executive board and twice past president of the New York State Psychological Association Division on Addictions. She publishes and lectures widely on the integration of psychoanalytic thought with harm reduction psychotherapy and substance use treatment.
Harm reduction therapy, harm reduction, substance use treatment, substance misuse, addiction, psychoanalysis

In this article, I describe Harm Reduction Therapy, the most current model for treating substance misuse, and I show how this approach is more consistent with psychotherapy and psychoanalysis than traditional substance use treatment has been. As opposed to the Disease Model, which has been the dominant approach, Harm Reduction welcomes anyone who wishes help with their substance use into treatment. Harm Reduction practitioners do not require that their patients embrace a goal of abstinence in order to enter treatment but work with each individual to establish the goals best suited to them. In addition, the harm reduction approach decenters substance use as a focus and instead considers the whole individual in treatment even when abstaining or moderating use is a primary goal of the work. The meaning and function of substance use is considered as well as the importance of psychodynamics, dissociation, self states and enactments. Harm Reduction therapy is based on a mutual, collaborative relationship between clinician and patient and much like any psychotherapy, the work takes place in the context of that relationship and the dynamics thereof. Clinical vignettes highlight how analytic work dovetails with substance use treatment in this relational harm reduction approach.

Bradley Jones   Graduate of two psychoanalytic institutes: The Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity (IPSS) in NYC, and The Institute for Contemporary Psychoanalysis (ICP/LA) in Los Angeles, CA. He is a Supervising Training Analyst and faculty at both institutes, and enjoys promoting the Explorations! series for IPSS. In private practice for over 30 years now, Bradley has a special interest in working with substance use and mis-use, people in the performing arts, and those who wish to explore alternative sexuality. He has published articles found in the journals Self, Context, and Psychoanalysis and Psychoanalytic Inquiry.
Gay, substance misuse, methamphetamine, psychoanalysis

Joe Ruggiero is known for starting a cutting-edge adult program at The Addiction Institute of Mount Sinai Hospital in New York City that focuses on the lives of gay men and their use of methamphetamine. The groups he created include men in various stages of substance use on the continuum of change and those working toward abstinence. I have always wanted to know more about Joe’s work, as I imagined he would have a trove of important insights around working with this difficult group of patients. I decided to interview Joe for this issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry, and I am so pleased I did. He does not disappoint. In our discussion, Joe helps us identify unique themes that emerge in working with this population. Joe also helps us to identify how contemporary psychoanalysis invites clinicians and their patients to be curious and interested in the “function” that crystal meth provides its user, and how enhanced self-reflection can create useful conversations that help patients reduce risk and find their way, if they choose, to significant change.

Liberating the Soul: Multiple Self-States and the Mystical in the Treatment of Substance Abuse

Noelle Burton Psy.D.

Noelle Burton

510 Narberth Ave, Merion Station, PA 19066, USA
burtonnm@yahoo.com
http://orcid.org/0000-0002-0439-3329

Noelle Burton   Graduate of the NYU Postdoctoral Program in Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy and an Associate Editor of Psychoanalytic Dialogues. She is a Founding Member, Faculty and Supervising Analyst at The Institute for Relational Psychoanalysis of Philadelphia; and Faculty, The Stephen Mitchell Relational Study Center. She is in private practice in suburban Philadelphia.
Substance abuse, addiction, dissociation, multiple self-states, mystical, Alcoholics Anonymous

There is a common feature linking together the efficacy of the developmental multiple self-state treatment of addictions, the therapeutic power and impact of Alcoholics Anonymous (and other Twelve Step groups), and the successful use of psychedelic medicines to treat substance abuse: they all set the stage for a mystical experience. This paper will focus on how psychoanalytic treatment cultivates aspects of mystical experience, specifically in the multiple self-state treatment of substance abuse. The mystical roots of AA, and how the Twelve Steps cultivate mystical experience is presented. My purpose is to sensitize clinicians to mystical elements, as well as facilitate their cultivation, in order to potentiate their impact, whether this work is used alone or in conjunction with psychedelic medicine. Some patients may experience spiritual losses in childhood which may foreclose a wholesome spirituality in adulthood and necessitates the analyst’s sensitivity, curiosity, and responsiveness. Clinical cases illustrate how self-state work cultivates mystical experiences, the emergence of the mystical in the course of treatment, as well as spiritual losses in childhood.

Addiction, compulsivity, therapy, languagegames, psychoanalysis

In this paper, the author addresses the problem of dissociation and intellectualization – an absence of affective centering – in the context of addiction treatment. In these scenarios, aversion of affect often becomes a way of life, such aversion itself unseen and de-registered even when patients are sober, in Alcoholics Anonymous or other programs. Such emotional “black holes” are difficult to address when they remain in awareness on the part of the analyst but not the patient; this can lead to the former’s potential alienation or frustration, in line with a patient whose longstanding dissociative distancing leaves them confused as to just what the analyst is seeking or asking of them. Here, the notion of disparate language games, a central concept of philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein, is employed to assist in examining the problem of disjunctive dialogue, with patients who have been discouraged or forbidden from identifying, let alone expressing their emotionality. Affective symbolizing and languaging are foreign tongues, so primal is their reflex to withdraw from or “manage” feeling-states, originating in grossly misattuned surrounds wherein the child’s traumatizations are disregarded and lost to words, and later in dyads. A vignette illustrates how frustration or anxiety emerging in the field can be analytic gold, when participants suddenly sense mutually “charged” moments: outlines of relationality. Here, therapists can disconfirm the intrapsychic nature of patients’ disavowal by modeling and examining their own subjective contributions, an invitation to a two-person world.

Beyond Behavior: A Neuroscience-Informed Approach to Addiction Treatment Focused on a Fulfilling Life

Michael B. Levin MD

Michael B. Levin

4900 Cherry Creek S. Dr. Suite G, Denver, CO 80246, USA
drmblevin@gmail.com

Michael B. Levin   Brings a unique and diverse array of expertise to his 23 years of private practice as an addiction psychiatrist in Denver. His professional journey began in electrical engineering, a discipline that continues to shape his perspective. Transitioning into medicine, he became an internist, practicing predominately in academics with a brief foray into the Indian Health Service. Driven by his commitment to enhancing lives, he pursued specialized training in psychiatry, including a fellowship in addiction. His approach is further enriched by five decades of meditation practice, two years of basic neuroscience research, and seven years of psychoanalytic training at the Denver Psychoanalytic Institute.
Addiction, anti-reward network, psychoanalysis, substance use

Current paradigms frame addiction primarily as a behavioral disorder, leading to treatment approaches focused on behavior modification and success measured solely by abstinence. This paper challenges this limited perspective by drawing on neuroscience and psychoanalysis to propose a novel framework that prioritizes achieving a fulfilling life as the ultimate goal, utilizing examination of subjective experience as the pathway. Neuroscience findings on reward/anti-reward dysregulation suggest three distinct brain configurations corresponding to three fundamental modes of living: a fulfilling life, a neurotic life, and an addictive life. While individuals naturally navigate between these states, one typically dominates. This paper redefines neurotic life, not as Freudian id-ego conflicts, but rather as the incessant pursuit of safety and certainty driven by feelings of lack, yearning, and fear that our society often perceives as normative. Furthermore, it argues that the behavior-centric approach can contribute to oscillations between addiction and neurosis commonly known as the “revolving door” of addiction. In contrast, the traditional psychoanalytic approach offers a more holistic path toward a fulfilling life. Its in-depth understanding of human suffering, emphasis on subjective experience, and use of the therapeutic alliance make it a valuable tool for addressing the underlying dynamics of addiction. This framework shift encourages a move beyond mere behavior modification toward facilitating a meaningful and satisfying life, ultimately offering a more sustainable and impactful approach to addiction treatment.

Addiction, social criticism, Fanon, Freud, identity, culture

This paper explores how addicts or “stoners” assume an anti-identity that offers a valuable space of critique of the culture. Many adolescents confront turbulent crossings in making their way from family to the culture at large. This is particularly true of those who grow up feeling marginalized from society. Using drugs in a committed way allows a person continually to change their consciousness, often in resistance to taking on a worldly lens felt to be hostile to their very being. Committed drug use is thus often less about managing emotions than it is about forging an ideology and assuming an identity, one which offers a dangerous but valuable space of critique. In exploring the phenomenon of what I am calling stonerism, I draw from Freud’s great treatise on our love/hate relationship with the culture Civilization and its Discontents (2010) as well as from the work of Fanon. I will also examine my own flirtation with stonerism as an adolescent, with the idea of illustrating through my own circumstances the insights and perils that come with living in a space of critique and assuming anti-identity.

Epilogue: Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Substance Use and Misuse

D. Bradley Jones Psy.D. LCSW

D. Bradley Jones

146 West 10th Street, #4B, NYC, NY 10014
drbradley1323@gmail.com

D. Bradley Jones   Graduate of two psychoanalytic institutes: The Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity (IPSS) in NYC, and The Institute for Contemporary Psychoanalysis (ICP/LA) in Los Angeles, CA. He is a Supervising Training Analyst and faculty at both institutes. In private practice for over 30 years now, Bradley has a special interest in working with substance use and mis-use, and people in the performing arts. He has published articles found in the journal Self, Context, and Psychoanalysis and Psychoanalytic Inquiry.

The authors included in this addition of Psychoanalytic Inquiry join a growing assembly of theorists who raise fascinating new questions about the treatment of substance use. Taking these various perspectives into consideration, we seem to be moving toward a new clinical sensibility around treating substance users that requires what William Coburn (2014) describes as an “unrelenting respect for the complexity of human experiencing … .” This clinical attitude embodies curiosity, compassion, flexibility, and an uncompromising reverence for the individual who enters our consulting rooms. It is a sensibility that challenges us as clinicians to be unremitting in our personal awareness of our own context-embedded biases about substance use. It also requires us to be mindful of our use of stigmatizing language, and to begin to shake off some of the lingering shibboleths that are associated with the traditional models that frighten substance users away from discussing their use with anyone. Additionally, when the going gets tough with a patient whose substance use has escalated, the analyst must be aware of their own anxiety-driven propensity to slide into bifurcated, anxious either/or thinking, and “Hurry up and do something!” interventions. All of these qualities work in a relentless pursuit of what Coburn describes as “grasping the feel of complexity” that would assist a clinician to tolerate the non-linear, often chaotic details that may accompany the treatment of those patients who are not yet ready for abstinence, and who remain on the continuum of substance misuse.

Coburn writes that if one immerses oneself in a psychoanalytic complexity sensibility “[t]here is really no turning back.” I believe this to be true for the psychoanalytic treatment of substance users. If we decide to take on the challenge of learning more about substance use from these contemporary, curious, and empathic perspectives, the more the traditional substance use models cease to make sense. Is substance use best understood only as a genetic disease? Is it an immutable condition that can only be treated but never cured? Is it true that psychological work cannot be sorted out until the patient is completely sober? Are patients fully “responsible” for their drug use?

About her book Steven Levy has written: “This is a book to be read alongside Freud’s Papers on Technique” (2018, p. 360). Ellen came to psychoanalysis as a second profession following twenty-five years as a middle school English teacher. Driven to Write

Ellen Pinsky Psy.D.

Ellen Pinsky

8 Maple Avenue, Cambridge, MA 02139
Epinsky14@gmail.com

Ellen Pinsky   Author of Death and Fallibility in the Psychoanalytic Encounter: Mortal Gifts (Routledge, 2017). About her book Steven Levy has written: “This is a book to be read alongside Freud’s Papers on Technique” (2018, p. 360). Ellen came to psychoanalysis as a second profession following twenty-five years as a middle school English teacher. She says her experience in the classroom with eleven and twelve year-olds taught her most of what she needed to know to become a creditable clinician. She is on the faculty at Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute (BPSI). In 2014 she was awarded BPSI’s Deutsch Prize for her essay “The Olympian Delusion.”
Mortality, exploitation, character, ethics, mourning, writing

In this essay, I tell my personal experience of my therapist’s sudden death, linking that stunning loss to my development as a writer, and also to a subject long-neglected: the analyst’s mortality. The profession’s striking evasion compounded my need to understand what the loss could mean in relation to psychoanalysis itself. Practical and ethical contradictions within our discipline can be represented by the double meaning of “mortal:” The analyst is vulnerable (he or she can die) and also fallible (he or she can err). The analyst’s mortality in both of these senses underlies the work at every moment – a robot or angel can’t do it. That same mortal nature, therapeutically powerful, also carries the potential for destruction. Thus, I was led to consider the issue of unethical behavior across a range, from mis-steps to crimes. Clarity about the loss and its nature has made writing, for me, a form of mourning.

Prologue: Memories and Reflections of Analytic Educators

Stephen B. Bernstein MD

Stephen B. Bernstein

146 Wallis Road, Chestnut Hill, MA 02467
stephenbernstein@icloud.com
http://orcid.org/0000-0001-6960-4177

Stephen B. Bernstein   Training and supervising analyst, and a former Chair of the Education Committee at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute. His analytic articles have centered on the preparation of patients for analysis and the transition from psychotherapy, and on how candidates and analysts can write more openly and deeply about their analytic work. He has also written on the analysis of patients with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).

When I was in analytic training years ago at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute (BPSI), our monthly academic or scientific meetings were often delivered by well-known outside analysts and discussed by our most senior local training analysts. The usual 200 members in the audience at this large institute were stratified in seating, not by edict but by custom. The training analysts sat up front, then other analyst members, and finally the recent graduates and candidates were in the rear. Over the years much has changed. Now, in a profound shift, the two or three discussants of our esteemed guest lecturers are often candidates, and where we sit is almost random. Increasingly many of our training committee chairs and the members of those committees are analytic graduates, in addition to the training analysts. Analytic trainees and graduates of our three-year Advanced Therapy Program (ATP) have an important voice in our Institute’s and Society’s direction. New opportunities for teaching and leadership are available at an earlier stage. This diffusion of responsibility is a manifestation of changes in how we understand analysis and analytic training. These earlier opportunities are the focus of the articles in this issue.

As candidates and recent graduates have moved to the front rows of the auditorium and have often taken the podium, we have come to see that these highly educated men and women brought with them talents to teach, lead and administrate. Those skills can be amplified and refined, as they are informed by the memories and reflections of our educational forebears. In this issue, analytic educators will write openly and transparently about their special projects, programs and career experiences.

Open writing about what we do as analysts or as analytic educators or leaders of educational programs is rare in our literature. We have been primarily trained in clinical work, and although we have observed how faculty teach in our seminars, other aspects of educational leadership have been more sequestered, the province of only our most revered elders. Newer generations of analysts are now being asked to assume educational and leadership roles and responsibilities. They can benefit from access to the lived experience of analytic educators, trying on the various opportunities that they may be offered or to which they may aspire, in order to chart the possible trajectories of their future careers. How would it be to lead an institution through a significant crisis or to change aspects of its culture? What would it be like to become the containing clinical, educational or administrative Director of a training institution? What it is like to be the Editor in Chief of an analytic journal? How might we bring back psychodynamic thinking to a hospital residency training program? How does a child analyst function? How might we engage undergraduate and graduate students in analytic ways of thinking?

Arden Rothstein   Faculty Member and Training and Supervising Analyst, Psychoanalytic Association of New York (PANY) and Chair of the Progression Committee of the American Psychoanalytic Association’s Department of Psychoanalytic Education. Deeply committed to psychoanalytic education at PANY, she was a member of the Education Committee for decades; served as Chair, Psychology Outreach (1989–1999); Chair, Scholarship and Research (2001–2005); Chair, Academic Affairs (2005–2009); and Chair, Student Progression Committee (2011–2017), as well as Clinical Professor, Department of Psychiatry, New York University Medical Center. She is the first author of four books and numerous papers on topics such as psychoanalytic education; integration of psychoanalytic and neuropsychological perspectives on learning disabilities and AD/HD; men’s responses to their partners’ elective abortions; and a variety of other clinical psychoanalytic topics.
Educational initiatives, case development, psychoanalytic writing, revision of candidate progression criteria, robust and transparent supervisory evaluation, curriculum revision

Reflecting on a lifetime of involvement with psychoanalytic education, the prompts for attending to four particular aspects are discussed: (1) helping candidates develop cases; (2) enhancing candidates’ writing; (3) reviewing and revising the curriculum with a small group of respected colleagues to make it more comprehensive and integrated; and (4) ensuring that candidates receive educationally optimal feedback that is robust, transparent and reflective of a collaborative developmental spirit. Relationships between the motivation to address some features of psychoanalytic education and limitations of my own candidacy are considered, as is the experience of envisioning, introducing and rolling out these initiatives. Publications that directly grew out of these educational programs are described, as are the stimuli for additional contributions.

Internalization processes—introjection and identification, mentalization, conflict pathology, developmental deficit, developmental process, psychoanalytic education

Reflecting on my evolving career led me to an appreciation of how my earliest interests and values were developed and applied in multiple ways. An older disturbed sibling created an interest in why people are as they are, and involvement in my parent’s social activism led to a commitment to helping fewer people but in deep ways. I was exposed in my earliest training to the fascinating aspects of earliest mother child interactions patterns. This led me to develop a growing interest in internalization processes, which then led to many varied career paths. While treating patients of varied ages over long courses of psychoanalysis, I also ran a normal nursery for infants and toddlers, taught about earliest development, immersed myself in the analytic scholarship, joined study groups about gender development and coordinating analytic and developmental processes, and later set up training programs to facilitate the internalizing processes in the younger generation. Being on editorial boards and engaging in longitudinal research added more layers of complexity to the understanding of processes of most interest to me. The beauty of a career in psychoanalysis is that it is forever interesting, enriching and growth producing.

Stephen B. Bernstein MD

Stephen B. Bernstein

146 Wallis Road, Chestnut Hill, MA 02467

Stephen B. Bernstein   Training and supervising analyst, and a former Chair of the Education Committee at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute. His analytic articles have centered on the preparation of patients for analysis and the transition from psychotherapy, and on how candidates and analysts can write more openly and deeply about their analytic work. He has also written on the analysis of patients with Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).

The writing of memoirs is inextricably tied to the ability to look ahead, but also to look backward, to confront change and the progression by which younger generations will overtake and replace us, as teachers, as academic leaders, and as the analysts and supervisors of our trainees.

Several years ago I attended a meeting at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute to celebrate and appreciate the retirement of a number of older analysts. It was the first time in my memory that such a sendoff had occurred. Each of these colleagues was spoken about with appreciation and gratitude. As I left, I realized that, for the first time, our organization was able to say goodbye to aging friends and colleagues. Our analytic community seemed to have matured to the extent that we could finally confront together the reality of separation and eventual death. We had become able to mourn as a group. However, this implied that, until that time, we had been avoiding this in our communal past.

Our ability to mourn together allows us to more robustly allow our future educational leaders to replace us, and at an earlier time than in the past. As the lists of new names taking on important roles in our local and national organizations are published, it is important that our experienced educators impart what they have learned to those who will replace them, and that all of us share in this process.

The authors in this issue have shown us what they have accomplished in their careers, and most have described how their interest in analysis and in their specific projects developed. They have also told us about what they have learned over the years, and those thoughts may guide others: what they liked and appreciated; what disappointed them; and what may have surprised or been revealed to them.

As an example, Randy Paulsen arrived at his leadership role with a sense of being an outsider: outside the Mormon church as the child of “apostate” parents who had left the church; outside as a practicing analyst, while also working as a teacher of meditation, a trained Balint group staff facilitator in teaching hospitals; and, at that time, as a non-training analyst confronting issues that had usually been dealt with only by those inside that group. His story is one of using and learning from this quality of being an outsider, neutral, allying with no one group, as various groups pressed for their own different solutions and remedies. This enabled him to bring various groups together. His frequent diary entries were his companion, as was his wife, at times, who would listen and help him reflect. He learned that change could only occur using small group meetings which build into an eventual larger group consensus.

Prologue: Notes on New Psychoanalytic Books

Daniel Goldin MFT Psy.D.

Daniel Goldin

1515 Hope Street, Suite 202, South Pasadena, CA 91030
daniel@danielgoldinpractice.com

Daniel Goldin   Currently serves as editor of Psychoanalytic Inquiry. He has published numerous articles and co-hosts the podcast The Conversation with Daniel Posner. Daniel’s book Storying in Psychoanalysis and the Everyday World will be published by Routledge early next year. Daniel is a training and supervising analyst affiliated with the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis in California.

Often a writer’s best ideas come out of reading the writing of others, sending them off on tangents beyond the limits of the page and beyond the limits of their prior theoretical thinking. This issue is an attempt to capture some of the energy that comes of one author reading the work of another before that energy is fully metabolized in a new paper or book. All the writers of this issue were asked to respond to a book adjacent to psychoanalysis that they found interesting and record their reactions without feeling the obligation to provide a direct assessment or review. The following are their marginal notations articulated in essay form.

Singer jumps off Cain’s Bittersweet: How Sorrow and Longing Make Us Whole, a book devoted to exploring the rarely discussed, complex emotion of bittersweetness. In lovely poetic prose, Singer brings the feeling into vivid experiential life by finding touchstones in his own life.

In The Self: Lost and Found, Magid seeks an understanding of the “self” by bringing Buddhism into dialogue with new enactavist, phenomenological thinking in contemporary philosophy by considering two books side by side. The first is Garfield’s Losing Ourselves. The second is a book by Siderits, Thompson, and Zahavi called Self, No Self: Perspectives from Analytical, Phenomenological, and Indian Traditions. In his passage through these pages, Magid finds the “self” provisionally in an instantiating flow, “constituted by the vicissitudes of relational and physical changes that have taken place over time.”

Civitarese provides a brilliant series of “notes in the margin” of Zahavi’s Husserl’s Legacy. Like Magid, Civitarese sees in the tradition of phenomenology started by Husserl (and reaching a kind of apotheosis in the works of Merleu-Ponty) tremendous relevance to psychoanalysis, in this case bolstering contemporary ideas drawn from Bionian field theory.

Riker pulls from his own experience working at his university with first generation, mostly Latin college students to add some theoretical armature to Rodriguez’s important series of case-studies in his book Know That You Are Worthy: Experiences from First-Generation College Graduates.

Mark Singer MD

Mark Singer

55 East 87th Street, New York, NY 10128

Mark Singer   Psychiatrist and psychoanalyst. His essays on themes of nostalgic experience, affective memory and the passage of time have been published and presented widely. He is in practice in New York City.
Bittersweet, longing, cherry blossom, baseball, springtime

I would like to thank Daniel Goldin, the editor of this journal, for inviting me to write this essay. The notion of the bittersweet has been a longstanding interest of mine that I have written about previously, and I was pleased to have the opportunity to offer some further thoughts on the topic given the prompt of Susan Cain’s evocative book, which at its essence, is about all the beauty that loss and longing afford. In my initial discussion with Daniel about the prospect of writing this piece, I referred to a prior essay that I had written some years ago about a national Vietnam War protest that I attended as a child with my family in Washington, D.C. In my memory of that event as I noted in that piece, “It seemed like the whole country was there that day. The scene felt chaotic but safe. And warm.” Sitting atop my father’s shoulders, the anti-war poster that stood out to me most read, “War is not good for children and other living things.” Daniel then told me that he was at that protest as a child as well, and that he too had sat on his father’s shoulders while listening to the speeches. He said, “We might have seen each other.” So this essay is for all the children who sat on the shoulders of their parents in protest of war on that day long ago, connected now in some bittersweet way, through our longing for childhood and an ongoing plea for peace.

Self, no self, personhood, Buddhism, phenomenology, intersubjectivity

Can we have experiences without a “self” that’s having them? Is my “self” something private and interior, unknowable to anybody else? How is that inner self related to my body, to other people, to the world? Questions like these can lead down a seemingly endless philosophical maze, yet psychologically important issues around identity, personhood, and ethical responsibility may hinge on how we consciously or unconsciously answer them. The books under review explore a range of ways of engaging these issues, from the Cartesian tradition in Western philosophy contrasted first with Buddhist psychology and then onto contemporary phenomenology to arrive at a pragmatic understanding of personhood grounded in intersubjectivity and relationality.

Although we have worked as analysts for many years, we still find that we are filled with distressing uncertainty about what the most healing response might be at crucial moments. Should we speak or remain silent? Should we ask questions or give answers? Should we disclose something of our own experience or allude to something that occurred between us and the patient in the past? Does one theory or another better address this situation?

Invariably we do respond even if we could not say what led us to the response we choose. We imagine that our choice has been guided, to some extent, by what we have learned from our teachers, supervisors and the writings of authors we prize. But from whom did our analytic progenitors gain their insights? In our efforts to trace the lineage of our guides to analytic practice we have come to believe that biblical and origin stories are a largely unrecognized source of therapeutic wisdom.

Even those of us who do not consciously draw on these stories have been influenced by them; they suffuse our worlds. We have learned that there is no known society that does not have an origin story and that these stories were not often created by solitary individuals but rather that they took form from repeated telling and retelling over many generations. The contributors to this issue have been inspired by these powerful stories and have used them in highly creative ways to better understand the psychoanalytic situation.

We open the issue with Daniel Goldin’s consideration of psychoanalytic origin stories. In “How the Socio/Political World Shapes our Psychoanalytic Origin Stories,” Goldin explores how the work of Sigmund Freud, Melanie Klein, Harry Stack Sullivan, Erich Fromm, Heinz Kohut, and Stephen Mitchell reflect turns of thinking that address serious disruptions in the cultures in which these theorists lived. He contends that a renewed interest in the cultural imprint on consciousness occupies many analysts today.

Next you will find “‘A Wrinkle in Time’: Serendipitous Creativity Between a 20th Century Psychoanalyst and a 16th Century Kabbalistic Rabbi” by Allen Siegel. He contends that although Heinz Kohut and Rabbi Isaac Lurya were separated by 500 years, and despite their very different experiences as Jews, both men endured the vulnerability of belonging to an unwanted people. In a creation myth of his own invention, Lurya suggested a theological process in which God needed Adam to restore the fractured Divine to its lost perfection. Heinz Kohut was concerned about addressing emotional fragmentation in human beings. Both men, according to Siegel, teach us about fragmentation, healing and the repair of a broken whole.

Myth, idealizing narcissism, mirroring narcissism, kinship narcissism, disruption, repair

This paper explores some ideas about narcissism that serendipitously were shared by two thoughtful men across a 500-year span of time. Separated by cultures and professions quite different from each other, the innate sensibilities, observations, and intelligent conclusions of these two very different men suggest a universality to the role of narcissism within the human condition. One man, Rabbi Issac Lurya (1534–1578), was a young, sixteenth century Kabbalistic theologian. The other man, Heinz Kohut (1914–1981) was a twentieth century psychoanalyst. Different as they were, these two men shared one set of similarities. Both men were Jews. Each lived in the immediate shadow of horrific antisemitic atrocities. Of significant interest is that the theory of each man deals with issues of fragmentation, healing, and repair of a broken whole. Psychoanalyst Heinz Kohut was concerned with the emotional fragmentation of a broken person and the restoration of emotional wholeness for that person. Rabbi Issac Lurya was concerned about the fragmentation of the shattered Divine and suggested a process to restore the broken Divine to its former perfection and through that restoration, to heal the Universe.

Blinded by the Light: The Double-Edged Sword of Idealization in Buddhist Origin Stories

Barry Magid MD

Barry Magid

211 Central Park West #One I, New York, NY 10024
bmmagid@gmail.com

Barry Magid   Faculty member of The Institute for Contemporary Psychotherapy and The Stephen Mitchell Relational Study Center, both in New York City and has served on the Executive Board of The International Association for Relational Psychoanalysis and Psychotherapy (IARPP). He is the editor of “Freud’s Case Studies: Self Psychological Perspectives” (1993) and the author of numerous articles on Self Psychology, most recently (co-authored with Estelle Shane and James Fosshage), “The Emerging Paradigm of Relational Self Psychology.” (2021) He is the founding teacher of the Ordinary Mind Zendo in New York, having received Dharma Transmission from Charlotte Joko Beck in 1998. He has written three books on the interface between Zen and Western Psychology: “Ordinary Mind: Exploring the Common Ground of Zen and Psychoanalysis” (2002), “Ending the Pursuit of Happiness” (2008), “Nothing is Hidden: The Psychology of Zen Koans” (2013) and edited (with Robert Rosenbaum) (2016) “What’s Wrong with Mindfulness (and What Isn’t).”
Buddhism, Zen, origin myths, idealization, cruel optimism

The life of the historical Buddha, and that of his successors in my own Zen tradition, come down to us as part hagiography and part mythology, amalgamated together both to teach particular spiritual lessons and to offer idealized models of the awakened life. Origin stories of this kind offer us a double-edged sword of idealization, one that establishes a goal that is simultaneously attractive and inspiring and at the same time, one so lofty, that by its very nature, may be made to appear unreachable. This paper explores problematic aspects of such stories in Buddhism, what Lauren Berlant has called “cruel optimism,” and describes some of the consequences when modern practitioners measure themselves against a myth.

Jeffrey Last PHD

Jeffrey Last   Clinical psychologist in private practice in Southfield Michigan. He earned his Ph.D. in clinical psychology from The George Washington University. He has published professional papers in the area of early memories as well as the interface between psychology and religion. He is the author of two books, Psychotherapy and Prayer and Four Essays in Psychology and Religion. He lives with his wife in Oak Park Michigan.
Biblical patriarchs, psychosexual development, psychotherapeutic technique, psychosocial development

The lives of the three patriarchs, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in Genesis can be seen as epitomizing three primary emotions, which in turn correspond to the first three psychosexual stages described by S. Freud and the first three stages of psychosocial development elucidated by Erickson. These three emotions are described in the mystical writings of the Zohar as Chesed (lovingkindness), Geuvra (personal strength), and Tiferes (integration). Parallels of these emotions with the first three stages of development described by Freud and Erikson are discussed. Case vignettes are presented in which patients’ struggles can be seen as reflecting these issues. Implications for therapeutic technique are also be discussed.

After “The Fall”: What the Bible Story Teaches Psychoanalysts About the Risks and Rewards of Embodied Relational Knowing

Doris Brothers PHD and Jon Sletvold Psy.D.

Jon Sletvold

65 West 90th Street, #3F, New York, NY 10024, U.S.A.
dorisbrothers@mac.com

Jon Sletvold   Founding board director of the Norwegian Character Analytic Institute. He is the author of The Embodied Analyst: From Freud and Reich to Relationality, 2014, winner of the Gradiva Award, 2015. His latest book, co-authored with Doris Brothers, is entitled A New Vision of Psychoanalytis Theory, Practice and Supervision: TALKING BODIES, Routledge Taylor and Francis, 2023. He is co-director with Doris Brothers of The Wilhelm Reich Center for the Study of Embodiment.
“The Fall”, relational knowing, confessions, meaning, recognition, knowledge/power

The biblical origin story of Adam and Eve, known as “the Fall,” is used as the basis for an exploration of what the authors call “embodied relational knowing.” This experiential realm includes the need to be known by others, the need to know others, and the need not to know or be known. The authors review Lewis Aron’s comparison of exegesis of the story by Erich Fromm and Rabbi Joseph Soloveitchik and compare relational knowing with the concepts of meaning and recognition. They address the ethical dangers of relational knowing with reference to Marcel Foucault’s writings on “knowledge/power.” Two illustrative clinical examples are provided.

The Power of Myth: Can Rediscovering the Sublime in Nature Solve the Climate Crisis?

Margy Sperry Psy.D. MFT

Margy Sperry

11340 Olympic Blvd. Suite 275, Los Angeles, CA 90064
Margysperry@gmail.com

Margy Sperry   Training and Supervising analyst at the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis in Los Angeles, and an international council member for the International Association of Psychoanalytic Self Psychology.
Myth, climate change, awe, sublime, nature, sacred

In Sacred Nature: Restoring our Ancient Bond with the Natural World, author Karen Armstrong contends that the damage that humanity is inflicting on the natural world reflects a severed link between the natural world and the sublime in Western cultures, where nature is viewed as a resource to be controlled and exploited. She contrasts this attitude with other religious traditions that venerate nature and see it as inseparable from the divine. In this article, I review Armstrong’s book and consider how Western socio-cultural attitudes and religious narratives collide with my love for the natural world, impacting my efforts to adopt more sustainable practices.

The articles in this issue leave little doubt that analysts would be well-served by revisiting biblical and origin stories. The enduring relevance of bible stories for the practice of psychoanalysis has been shown in the work of Allen Siegel, Jeffrey Last, Melvin Bornstein, and Doris Brothers and Jon Sletvold. The ways in which our own and our patients’ personal narratives are influenced by culture, history and the socio-political surround have been amply demonstrated by Barry Magid’s examination of Buddhist origin stories and Daniel Goldin’s exploration of psychoanalytic origin stories. By reviewing Karen Armstrong’s survey of religious traditions that honor the divine in nature, Margy Sperry provides us with glimmers of hope that our efforts to save our precious earth from human-inflicted damage will succeed.

Despite the broad variety of these articles, they have barely made a dent in the enormous trove of origin story treasures that await discovery. We hope that analysts have been inspired to search for them.

[[RunningHead]]

Prologue: Framing the Impact of the Global Pandemic on the Child and Adolescent Treatment Process

Jackie Gotthold Psy.D.

Jackie Gotthold

330 West 58th Street, Suite 201, New York, NY 10019
Jackie.gotthold@gmail.com

Jackie Gotthold   Affiliated with the Institute for the Psychoanalytic Study of Subjectivity (IPSS), in New York City, where she serves on the Executive Committee and is a faculty member, supervisor and training analyst. Jackie teaches and presents at psychoanalytic conferences and institutes globally. Jackie is a member of IAPSP, and IARPP. Her current research interests include: Psychoanalytic clinical process working with children and adolescents, the integration of infant research into the psychoanalytic clinical process and integration one’s personal psychoanalytic clinical theory.

An unfathomable scenario – a global pandemic – impacts psychoanalysis – the consultation, confidentiality, the felt intimacy, the predictability, the startling “moments” and the affective engagement. As a field known for its glacially slow change process, we were impacted as if struck by a meteor.

Can we remember the events of those initial weeks and months?

It is not surprising that everyone clamors to recount those moments and days when the realization or rather trauma hit. We all tell and re-tell those moments, as we do with traumatic events, in the service of mastery and perhaps healing.

Remember the feelings?

In New York City, on March 13, 2020, the music, the noise and as Amy Joelson (this issue), one of our authors notes, for child and adolescent psychotherapists, the play stopped. The “shutdown” took place on the eve of many Spring Break school vacations. So many clinical dyads bid goodbye for two weeks, anticipating or hoping for a resumption of connection at the end of “break.” As the full scope of what a pandemic meant, as professional identity and even existence were called into question, the lack of preparation sent everyone scrambling.

Abrupt, destabilizing and frightening, the COVID-19 virus and the resulting global pandemic reconfigured, and I might assert, forever altered our clinical approach – logistically and theoretically. “Lockdowns,” “social distancing,” “masking” and toy washing were suddenly part and parcel of the child/adolescent clinical exchange. Hoping to limit “transmission” of the virus, clinicians were, at times required and at other times urged to follow medical? governmental? common sense?, guidelines around how we “see patients.” So, as clinicians, we found ourselves participating in a lightening fast, experientially disorienting, move to the “virtual” or “remote” consultation room – the ‘Zoom Room.’ This phrase, and many others, expanded and became newly embedded in the clinical lexicon. The move to “remote,” a word that is the antithesis of our clinical endeavor, presented as now a means of connection.

The Manifest Dream Reconsidered

Rebecca Smith Behrends PHD

Rebecca Smith Behrends

Rebecca Smith Behrends   Assistant Professor of Psychiatry at the Yale University School of Medicine and an advanced psychoanalytic candidate at the Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis.
Manifest dream, latent content, secondary revision, mental representation, traumatic experience

The purpose of this paper is a reexamination of the concept of the manifest dream. First, the major tenets of Freud’s distinction between manifest and latent content will be reviewed, together with his recommendations for dream interpretation which follow from that distinction. Second, I will attempt to identify problematic philosophical assumptions which appear to be inherent in both the clinical theory and the metapsychology of the manifest dream. Next, I will highlight examples from Freud’s writing which suggest that Freud himself remained ambivalent about the degree of significance which should legitimately be accorded the manifest content of dreams. Finally, I will suggest an alternative theoretical framework for approaching the manifest dream, and manifest content in general, utilizing the concept of the representational world as the basic organizing construct.

Zahavi, Husserl, intersubjectivity, intercorporeality, we-perspective, post-Bionian field theory

The author examines Dan Zahavi’s study of Husserlian philosophy, tracing Husserl’s transition from an early solipsistic position to the later development of a radical intersubjective view. He examines the concept Husserl invented of intersubjectivity, highlighting its development and influence on Heidegger, Nancy, Merleau-Ponty, and Derrida. The main thesis is that his speculative view of the complex relationship between self, other, and world deepens the understanding we may have of intersubjectivity in our discipline. Although the author does not advocate Husserl’s ontology for psychoanalysis, he argues that Husserl’s understanding is essential for dealing with this concept in contemporary psychoanalysis, and especially for examining the congruity between approaches that define themselves as intersubjective and the technique used in clinical work. In this perspective, the author offers a critical analysis of Donnel Stern’s conceptualization of post-Bionian field theory and its differences with interpersonal models, highlighting some convergences but also some points of contention.

Queer, identity, LGBT, queerphobia, transphobia, regulatory anxiety

This paper uses psychoanalytic methodology to interrogate queerphobia. Through the sharing of a brief encounter with a prospective patient who insisted on knowing whether or not the analyst was a “gay man” despite the analyst already having identified himself as a “queer person,” the regulatory anxieties and violence attendant to queerphobia are explored. Clinical and theoretical questions related to identity, both in therapist-patient fit and in the identity paradigm more broadly, are considered through a critical examination of the exchange between analyst and prospective patient. Borrowing from the work of Jill Gentile, the feminine and the vaginal are taken up as organizing/disorganizing paradigms in both methodology and content as the caller’s insistence is explored. The deployment of logics of biology as a rhetorical move is also investigated here, as the caller continues to push the question of whether the analyst is a “biological” gay man. In an attempt to think beyond the analyst’s failures in initiating treatment with the caller, as well as the caller’s queerphobia, the author leans on the notion of queer potentiality as developed by José Esteban Muñoz to dream forward another, more generative version of the interaction.

[[RunningHead]]

Having No Idea and Many Ideas at the Same Time: Emergence, Continuity, and Dissonance in Cultural Frames of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity

Nicole Warner Psy.D. LPCC LMFT

Nicole Warner

949 University Avenue, Suite 101, Sacramento, CA 95825
NicoleNelsonMFT@gmail.com

Nicole Warner   Part of the faculty at the Institute of Contemporary Psychoanalysis in Los Angeles, California where she serves as co-chair on the Task Force to Address Racism and Homophobia, and co-teaches the course “Psychoanalytic Perspectives on Diversity, Power, and Privilege.” She works in private practice in Sacramento, California where she works with LGBTQIA+, neurodiverse, and individuals coping with severe trauma and dissociation.
Heteronormative, LGBTQ+, gender identity, sexual orientation, frames

We are surrounded by heteronormativity, heteronormativity that as primary frame organizes our experiences around sexual orientation and gender identity and does not leave much room for exploration of subjective experiences regarding gender and sexual orientation. Immediately, and often before we can even register our subjective experiences, we find ourselves thinking in terms of identity categories that have been socially constructed to both conform to and resist the dominant heteronormative frame. This paper explores some of the history of the heteronormative frame, the value of counter-frames (frames that resist or modify socially constructed dominant frames) as well as the possibility of stepping into ambiguity and going “frame-less.” A clinical example is presented of a previously thought to be heterosexual couple, as one member of the couple shifts gender identity categories. This clinical work illustrates the possibilities that can emerge when therapists hold the tension between the need for identity categories and the necessarily limiting nature of these categories.

Paul   Charles Howard Candler Professor of Anthropology and Interdisciplinary Studies; Adjunct Professor in the Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences; Teaching and Supervising Analyst, Emory University Psychoanalytic Institute; Dean Emeritus, Emory College of Arts & Sciences; and Director Emeritus, Emory University Psychoanalytic Institute.
Emory, institutes, didactic training, Arts & Sciences, candidates, graduate students

After recounting my journey from being a professor at Emory University to becoming a practicing psychoanalyst, while maintaining my career as a professor, I turn to a comparison of psychoanalytic education and doctoral education in the Arts & Sciences. I relate many of these contrasts to differences in the institutional arrangements in which each takes place, and I note the attractions and impediments to analytic training for those in an academic career. I advocate for licensure to accompany graduation from an analytic institute, arguing that current regulations in many states prevent academics who might otherwise do so from becoming clinicians because they are not licensed. Closer relations between psychoanalysis and the university can only be to the benefit of both.

Diana Diamond PHD and Kay M. Long PHD

Kay M. Long

135 Central Park West, New York, NY 10023
ddiamonda@gmail.com

180 East Rock Road, New Haven, CT 06511
kay.long@yale.edu

Kay M. Long   Associate Clinical Professor of Psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine and a Training and Supervising Analyst at The Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis.

This memorial issue entitled Internalization, Self-Other Differentiation, and Relatedness: The Enduring Legacy of Sidney J. Blatt is an issue of remembrance and appreciation that includes scholarly and research papers as well as personal reflections by the contributors on the ways that Sid influenced their professional and personal development. The issue features papers by several generations of Sid’s colleagues and mentees that reflect key aspects of his work. In the spirit of Sid’s international work and collaboration during his career, the contributors are a global group representing Israel, Belgium, the UK, as well as North America.

This issue commemorates the 10th anniversary of Sid’s death. In the past 10 years Sid’s work has only become more relevant and central for the fields of developmental and clinical psychology and psychoanalysis. His legacy lives on in numerous areas of contemporary psychoanalytic discourse, including 1) the articulation and expansion of object relations theory to encompass findings from social, cognitive, and attachment perspectives; 2) the idea that personality development evolves through the hierarchical synergistic interaction of the two vectors of self-definition and relatedness, with increasingly mature relatedness fostering increasing self-definition over the life span (the two-configurations model); 3) the idea that psychopathology involves distortions in self-and object representations stemming from hypertrophy of one developmental line at the expense of the other; 4) the development of empirical methods to assess the developmental quality and structural characteristics of mental representations both conscious and unconscious and the way they change over the course of treatment; 5) the conceptualization and treatment of depression beyond narrow DSM5 or ICD diagnostic approaches; and 6) the understanding of internalization as a core process in early development and in psychotherapeutic change. Given these colossal contributions, it is no wonder that this issue follows a cascade of tributes.
