Susan McNamara   Analyst and former co-chair of the Committee on Gender and Sexuality of the American Psychoanalytic Association. She is on the faculty of the Metropolitan Institute for Training in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy and Yale School of Medicine and a Consulting Editor of Psychoanalytic Inquiry.

The summer of 2023 was upon New York City. Taylor Swift (2023) started the party in May with her Eras Tour, with the Bronx rapper Ice Spice joining her onstage. Restaurant sheds left on the streets were packed with New Yorkers enjoying their favorite craft brews. The Pride March ended at a dance party at the Brooklyn Army Terminal in Sunset Park headlined by Christina Aguilera (2023) singing “Lady Marmalade” while dressed in a rainbow rhinestone jumpsuit with Adam Lambert wearing green leopard-skin. Flaco, the escaped Eurasian eagle-owl, explored the city from on high, refusing to let himself be captured by zoo employees. The sex therapist, Dr. Ruth Westheimer, lamented that poor Flaco was “flying all over New York to find companionship” (Shanahan, 2024). City pools were open again. The ferry to Fire Island was crowded. The Jersey Shore was packed.

The season’s marquee event was the Beyoncé Renaissance tour at the end of July. It was all over the news, it was all over the internet, and sound systems around the city rocked to “Break My Soul” (Beyoncé, 2022) and what Wesley Morris described as music “steeped in or conducted entirely with Black queer bravado” (2022). Fans turned out in fringed cowboy hats and megawatt sparkles as transit employees shouted, “Beyoncé, Track 14!” (Holtermann & Hamja, 2023). NJ Transit posted memes of buses and trains wearing glittering silver cowboy hats. Beyoncé is known for great dance numbers, and according to J Wortham (2023):

During “Pure/Honey,” there’s a moment when the stage transforms into a soul-train lineand ballroom stage. And then Beyoncé does something extraordinary: She switchesbodies with her dancers. Which is to say, she trades places with them, turning her back on the main stage (a full-body mic drop), and lets her tremendous team of dancers inherit herplace. The dancers, emboldened by the spotlight, take turns vogueing and cat-walkingdown the stages. It is one of the most triumphant moments of the tour. (2023)

In early July, a new multicultural Barbie movie was released, far queerer than anyone would ever imagine. Its big dance numbers are reminiscent of the heyday of Hollywood soundstage musicals (Gerwig, 2023). The music was loud, and New York City was dancing.

In her published writing, Andi has explored the role of the internet as atransitional space for transgender and gender-diverse adolescents and adults, the impact of familial and sociocultural contexts on LGBTQ+ identities, and the interplay between social and psychic structures in the pandemic era. She was the recipient of the 2023 Ralph E.Roughton Award and is an editorial associate with the Journal of the American Psychoanalytic Association (JAPA). Andi serves on APsA’s Committee on Gender and Sexuality (COGS) Task Force to Combat Misinformation and Bias.
Charitable hatred, spiritual violence, religious trauma, LGBTQ+, futurity, resilience

Queer studies have flourished in psychoanalysis in recent decades, but surprising lacunae remain. Little has been written on the role of religious trauma and spiritual violence in queer lives. The author explores the psychic reverberations of spiritual violence, especially as it manifests through Christian supremacy and “charitable hatred.” A brief history of “charitable hatred” is discussed and linked to the current sociopolitical atmosphere in the United States where legislative attacks on LGBTQ+ rights have been on a dramatic rise. Links between homotransphobia within fundamentalist Christianity and conservative psychoanalysis are examined. Through case material, the author explores the traumatic sequelae of “charitable hatred” and the resilience involved in navigating this dangerous psychic and relational territory while holding on to what Winnicott called “continuity of being.” The potentiality of the analytic relationship in opening space for a patient’s compromised sense of futurity is also explored.

Susan Donner   Psychoanalyst, a Clinical Instructor at the Yale School of Medicine, and a past recipient of the Ralph Roughton Paper Award.
Parenting, LGBTQ+, child development, families, gayby boom

What is it like being an LGBTQ+ parent? In June 2017, the American Psychoanalytic Association Committee on Gender and Sexuality sponsored a discussion group in the format of a round table that primarily included LGBTQ+ psychoanalysts speaking on the joys and challenges of parenting in a heteronormative world. (The + is used metaphorically to capture all the identities that fall outside traditional gender norms.) The goal of the discussion group was to describe the impact of all types of family relationships on child development and demonstrate how to foster a social environment in which all children and their families are valued, experience support and recognition, and in which discrimination and prejudice have no place. We are pleased to finally publish this updated paper, which is dedicated to the memory of Don Spivak, whose commitment to the welfare of children is dearly missed.

Parenting, development, gender, gender variance, gender identity, gender fluidity

Parenting gender variant children presents challenges both to parents’ internal development and to their tasks of parenting. Although there is a burgeoning literature on many topics regarding transgender development and experience, there is little that directly addresses parents’ internal emotional experience of their child’s gender variance. In this article, parent development and parenting tasks particularly relevant to parenting children with “differences” are reviewed, along with Diane Ehrensaft’s delineation of parent experience with gender variant youth. Next, assumptions and biases are considered. Then, as the central focus, I describe and discuss my own journey with a gender variant child, augmented by the experiences of others.

Autotheory, transgender, detransition, trans exclusionary radical feminism, self analysis, queer theory

From a first-person narrative describing transition, detransition, and retransition, I describe my experience with gender and sexuality. In providing these experiences, I implement the feminist methodology of autotheory. This methodology uses personal experience through narrative and poetry as a mode for theory production and a device to critically examine oppression. As a psychoanalytic model of inquiry, this methodology has not been used for investigating transgender experience. The experience of gender transition is rarely described in the first person in psychoanalytic literature. This lack within the psychoanalytic field has resulted in psychoanalytic representations of transition that negatively impact transgender people. My experience covers an elaboration of both problematic conceptions of gender and sexuality within psychoanalysis, the difficulties associated with trans-exclusionary radical feminism, and coming to terms with gender and sexuality through queer activism. Implementing this narrative form, I speak back to psychoanalysis via an autotheoretical feminism purposed for relational psychoanalytic thought. In conclusion, I provide a means to grasp trans experience through psychoanalytic formulation. I propose the processes of gendered experience are relational and malleable within communities; embodied through systems of violence and oppression; and personal-political experiences.

Cary Friedman MD

Cary Friedman

875 Massachusetts Avenue, Suite 51, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA
caryfriedman@verizon.net

Cary Friedman   President-Elect and a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute. An earlier version of this paper was awarded the Institute’s 2012 Felix and Helene Deutsch Prize. He is a past Lecturer, Part-time at Harvard Medical School, and a member of the American Psychoanalytic Association Committee on Gender and Sexuality.
Homosexuality, psychoanalysis, theory of sexuality, gay men, history, prejudice

Since Sigmund Freud began his revolutionary text Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality in 1905 with a detailed study of homosexuality, our efforts to understand same-sex attraction and behavior have played a central role in psychoanalytic theory. This paper describes the historical evolution of four psychoanalytic paradigms of male homosexuality – Freud’s search for understanding, homosexuality as illness, homosexuality as health, and the deconstruction of categories of illness and sexuality. A close examination of the underlying assumptions of each paradigm shows the strong influences that cultural context and prejudice have had on psychoanalytic theory and the need for tolerance of uncertainty as a core psychoanalytic value. A clinical illustration of the author’s work with a gay man explores the continuing influence of discredited theories in the minds of patients, and how subsequent theories can be useful in helping patients establish a cohesive and affirmative sexual identity, while also allowing for fluid notions of sexual identity.

“We Pass for What We Are”: Otherness and Humanness

Joy Ladin PHD

Joy Ladin

143 Bennett Avenue 4R, New York, NY 10040
joyladin@gmail.com

Joy Ladin   Nationally known writer and speaker on transgender identities and issues whose numerous books include a phenomenological memoir of gender transition, Through the Door of Life, and an exploration of the theological implications of transgender experiences of otherness, The Soul of the Stranger.
Otherness, difference, double-consciousness, transgender

There is a wide-ranging academic literature addressing “Otherness” from sociological, philosophical, pedagogical, psychological, and literary perspectives, but there is little work that distinguishes between kinds of Otherness, nor much systematic exploration of the intersection between the social dynamics that produce, and the psychological effects of experiencing, different kinds of Otherness. As a result, psychotherapists often lack both the vocabulary and conceptual tools they need to respond to transgender, nonbinary, or other clients whose lives and psyches have been shaped by the experience of Otherness. By reading personal experiences of Otherness as a transgender child living in hiding and an adult “othered” by gender transition through the lenses of theoretical concepts of Otherness developed by W.E.B. Du Bois, Jean-Francois Staszak, and Ralph Waldo Emerson, this essay seeks to expand our conceptual vocabulary for, and practical therapeutic understanding of, the varieties and effects of feeling and being seen as Other. This essay argues that we need to understand Otherness simultaneously as a social circumstance many of us need to cope with, a psychic wound, and a formative sense of difference which, even as it makes us feel isolated, gives each human being something in common with everyone around us. To this end, this essay delineates three distinct, interrelated forms of Otherness – Structural Otherness, Internalized Otherness, and Inherent Otherness – including their psychological effects, the social dynamics that foster them, and how each represents an effort to understand ourselves in ways that enable us to relate and attach to those to whom our difference marks us as Other.

Queering Up Psychoanalysis – An Integrative Model with the Power to Meet the Moment

Francis Novak D.Psa. L.C.S.W.-R

Francis Novak

80 8th Avenue, Suite 1303, New York, NY 10011
fran.novak@gmail.com

Francis Novak   Psychoanalyst in private practice in New York City. He trained at the Manhattan Institute for Psychoanalysis and is a Postdoctoral Fellow at the Parkmore Institute. He is a founding member and the Principal Clarinetist of the Queer Urban Orchestra. He is on faculty at the Manhattan Institute for Psychoanalysis and the Institute for Expressive Analysis.
Queer theory, existentialism, archetypes, enactment, self-states, Golden Girls theory

Psychoanalysis is trying to meet the moment in a variety of ways on a variety of psychosocial issues. This paper explores the existential and human identity ramifications that most reflect rapid social, cultural, and global change. The impacts of climate change, years of global pandemic, domestic, and international terrorism, as well as war and nuclear threats are on all of our minds and on the minds of our patients. All pose as existential threats. The urgency that these threats inspire have palpably and overtly shaken our identities. In this paper, I argue that crisis is an opportunity to deconstruct and make meaning and has always been the biggest catalyst for change on all levels. It is an opportunity for growth, evolution, and redefinition. The parallel processes of global, social, and macro-level identity crises reflect the identity crises we are contending with on the individual and intrapsychic level. Culturally we are witnessing an abundance of artistic creation with the subject of identity, the multiplicity of identities, and intersectionality. In this paper, I examine contemporary art forms such as television and literature to demonstrate the centrality of human identity as the necessary path forward in our relation to existential crisis. As the theory of everything in physics would unify and string together the four fundamental interactions of nature, this paper would unify and string together the four fundamental parts of the human psyche.1 This paper elucidates the existence of the four primary self-states and the cruciality of their integration.

Trans Psychoanalysis and the High Court

Alex Colston MA

Alex Colston

3606 Bethoven Street, Apartment 1, Pittsburgh, PA 15213
colstonalex3@gmail.com

Alex Colston   Writer, the deputy editor of Parapraxis, co-director of The Psychosocial Foundation, and a clinical psychology Ph.D. student at Duquesne University.
Trans desire, Tavistock, law, politics, treatment

In 2020, Britain’s High Court passed a landmark ruling stating that persons under the age of 16 could not provide informed consent to receive puberty blocker treatment. This historically marked the resurgence of a long-standing and arduous struggle between trans-affirming organizations in the UK and the state. The clinical aspect of this political struggle played out at Tavistock and Portman, a foundation trust of the NHS that has long provided mental health services and gender-affirming care. In this article, by analyzing the medical concept of “Gillick competence,” I criticize the normative clinical and political reasons pressed into service in the lawsuit and in the institutional denial of gender- and trans-affirming psychotherapeutic care. I draw upon the work of Jacques Lacan, Jules Gill-Peterson, Paul Verhaeghe, Patricia Gherovici, and the late Mari Ruti to offer a different conception of psychoanalytic practice, one more avowedly friendly to trans desire. When practiced with sufficient theoretical rigor and playful open-endedness, I contend that psychoanalysis is a practice uniquely situated for learning to listen to and countenance trans desire.

responseSet.title: There is a Show Tune for Every Occasion: My Psychoanalytic Journey Through the Wonders of Musical Theater
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

There is a Show Tune for Every Occasion: My Psychoanalytic Journey Through the Wonders of Musical Theater

Cary Friedman MD

Cary Friedman

875 Massachusetts Avenue, Suite 51, Cambridge, MA 02139
caryfriedman@verizon.net

Cary Friedman   President-Elect and a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Boston Psychoanalytic Society and Institute. He is the recipient of the Institute’s 2012 Felix and Helene Deutsch Prize. He is a past Lecturer, Part-time at Harvard Medical School, and a member of the American Psychoanalytic Association Committee on Gender and Sexuality.
Musical theater, show tunes, psychoanalysis, Broadway, Stephen Sondheim, Lin-Manuel Miranda

Musical theater can enthrall our senses, captivate our hearts, and transport us to magical worlds. It can also offer profound and moving insights about intrapsychic states, the intricacies of human relationships, and the effects of our social surround on the human condition. By recounting his lifelong love of musicals, particularly the works of Stephen Sondheim and Lin-Manuel Miranda, the author describes how such deeply stirring and thought-provoking musical theater moments have enriched his psychoanalytic understanding of his patients’ and his own life journeys.

responseSet.title: Aaja Nachle: A Queer of Color Qualitative Study on Psychoanalysis, Gender, and Sexuality
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Aaja Nachle: A Queer of Color Qualitative Study on Psychoanalysis, Gender, and Sexuality

Murad M. Khan MD

Murad M. Khan

murad.khan@yale.edu

Murad M. Khan   Psychiatrist and psychoanalytic candidate at The Western New England Institute for Psychoanalysis. They received their B.A. from Yale University, M.D. from Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai, and completed their psychiatry residency at Yale University. They have presented on the mental health concerns of QTBIPOC for the American Psychiatric Association, the American Psychological Association, the American Psychoanalytic Association, and the Association of LGBTQ+ Psychiatrists. They are first author of the chapter on Gender and Sexual Identities in The Psychiatry Resident Handbook – How to Thrive in Training.
Psychoanalysis, gender, sexuality, queer of color critique, intersectionality

This project was initially conceived as a qualitative study investigating how current psychoanalysts think about gender and sexuality. As a second-year psychiatry resident considering psychoanalytic training, I was anxious about entering a community with so few QTBIPOC. On the other hand, much of my community organizing work drew inspiration from literature that had roots in psychoanalysis. I decided to conduct this study to reconcile this discrepancy, hoping my findings might be useful to others within and outside the psychoanalytic community. I conducted semi-structured interviews with 15 adult and 15 adult/child psychoanalysts (12 cis men, 16 cis women, 2 non-binary; 22 straight, 5 gay, 2 bisexual, 1 questioning; all white) who had completed psychoanalytic training and worked with at least one LGBTQ-identifying patient. In addition to sharing my findings using reflexive thematic analysis, I share my personal experience of the process. Drawing on queer of color critique, I use the metaphor of dance to illustrate how the participants and I reenacted familiar oppressive dynamics. I conclude by situating this project as an interpersonal representation of psychoanalysis’ ongoing participation in oppression.
